#6867. Under the Surface

Canali gives a behind-the-scenes look at sartorial excellence: the time, precision and mastery that transform raw materials into a jacket made to last

Under the surface, unseen layers lie. They stay there, silent. They don’t demand the spotlight. They don’t seek glory. And yet, like a beating heart, they form the innermost foundation of any real achievement. Where passion, enthusiasm, and discipline meet, the logic of excellence takes shape. Such is the story of Under the Surface, the newest creative collaboration from Canali.

Under the Surface is a look at the unseen architecture of a sartorial jacket by Canali. Every Canali jacket is born from a complex system of about 200 steps, each executed with meticulous care. Around 15 specialists are involved in the process—one that sees more than 520 feet of thread sewn into 22,000 stitches, both machine- and hand-made. Unseen when looking at the finished garment, the process informs each piece’s quality, comfort, shape, and durability.

It’s not just a matter of talent: rather, it’s about staying faithful to one’s goals, pursuing them with dedication even when no one is watching. It’s then that quality truly makes a difference, and the end result becomes the visible manifestation of a long creation process that demands great effort, experience and willpower.

That commitment of excellence unites the sartorial world of Canali and Ethan Hawke, the brand’s new Global Ambassador. The actor, writer, and director has dedicated almost four decades to perfecting his art, with endless, ever-learning curiosity. For their new Fall/Winter 2026 campaign, Canali has decided to capture what goes on behind the scenes. In the film, Hawke pores over his scripts, rehearses lines, refines each motion: a painstaking introspective process made of research, study, and exercise, preceding each of his performances.

The behind-the-scenes of a Canali jacket starts with selecting the finest fabrics, sourced from the best Italian wool mills. Then, each textile is examined and interpreted. While technology now allows extreme precision and control, some assessments are still left to the eye and expertise of human specialists. Even tiny details such as slightly different shades of color or variations in texture can influence the final product.

The fabric is then stabilized via steaming cycles and specific treatments, to ensure its behavior remains consistent over time. Then it’s time for digital mapping, guiding every cutting room decision: here, each of the jacket’s pieces is carefully positioned to also help keep waste to a minimum. It’s the first irreversible step.

The garment’s three-dimensional structure is then shaped upon the canvas. Canali crafts theirs in-house, adapting it to each model’s fit and fabrics. Made from horsehair, plant fibers, and natural reinforcements, the canvas is modeled on custom-made concave shapes, known as Schiena d’Asino (Donkey’s Back), which replicate the chest’s anatomy. The canvas is crucial for determining how a jacket drapes over the body, avoiding stiffness. It’s here that the volume of the chest, the balance of the silhouette and ease of wearing begin to be defined.

Then it’s time to craft the front, lapel, padded shoulder, and the sleeves. From planning to execution, nothing’s left to chance. The tailor observes, corrects, iterates. It’s a patient process, requiring time, knowledge, and skill. Lastly, the various layers are united through basting, stitching, and ironing processes. As these details interact, the garment takes on its structure and sophisticated character.

Something special also takes place behind the scenes with Hawke: day after day, the actor’s preparation subtly transforms his thoughts and behavior until, almost by instinct, he takes on each role’s intimate characteristics.

Time underpins the whole process. After being assembled and pressed, the jacket is allowed to rest, to dissipate the steam and stabilize the cloth. This is how the fabric finds its balance, and the garment gains a sort of memory: the ability to naturally find its shape again, even after having been worn, folded, or packed into a suitcase.

In over 90 years of heritage, Canali has refined their techniques through repetition, experience, and experimentation. Each garment is built upon the time-tested values of care, know-how, precision. The Canali style is not one made of grand gestures, but daily practice, intimate and subtle: the constant research into a shape that lasts. One hero of the Under the Surface project is the vicuña jacket, available exclusively at selected flagship boutiques by Canali.The campaign, and the collaboration between Canali and Ethan Hawke, speak to the art of shaping oneself, guided by an ambition to do things well with patience and self-awareness. Both in tailoring and in cinema, there is so much quiet work that happens behind the scenes to make creativity possible. Discipline and rigour do not constrain creative freedom; they make it possible. For Canali, excellence takes shape through the craftsmanship with which each element is made. For Ethan Hawke, it is the preparation that allows him to approach each role with confidence.And, as the Under The Surface campaign reveals, each of these steps adds something essential to the finished product. In the case of the Canali cashmere and vicuña blazer (the hero style of the FW26 campaign), it is structure, movement, character, durability, and a lightness that can only be achieved through the combination of expertly-chosen materials and complex fine tailoring. The knowledge required to execute this is almost tangible, felt in the quality of the piece.

The finished result only has value because of the strong, unseen structure underneath. It is a story we can all resonate with. Little by little, layer by layer, day by day, we each build ourselves in pursuit of excellence. Our actions create the people we are – even, or especially, when nobody is watching – in the same way that the apparent simplicity of a piece of clothing hides the depth of work required to craft it. This is the essence of Under the Surface.

#6862. Is Black Doves Returning for Season 3?

The Keira Knightley–led spy thriller finally returns to Netflix with a cliff-hanger that demands more episodes.

This story contains spoilers for the season 2 finale of Black Doves.

Black Doves was immediately one of the best spy thrillers on Netflix when it premiered two years ago. Unlike The Night Agent’s stilted acting and Reacher’s nonstop machismo, the British drama featured stellar acting from Keira Knightley in her most prominent role since her last Pirates of the Caribbean film. But after a year passed by without any new episodes or updates, I figured the spy series would never return.

Luckily, Netflix eventually gave Black Doves the green light and season 2 debuted in full on the streamer on Thursday, November 5. Alongside Ben Whishaw as hitman Sam Young, Knightley returns as Helen Webb, a global spy for hire who sells information to the highest bidder. She also happens to be the UK prime minister’s wife—which is not ideal when you’re trying to keep secrets.

In the first season, Helen also had to manage an affair that turned sour when her lover, Jason, was murdered. He was later revealed to be an MI5 agent sent to investigate her—you really can’t trust anyone if you’re a spy—but solving his murder was just the start of Helen’s problems. By the season 1 finale, audiences learned that the nanny who takes care of her children is also a spy.

The plot continues in season 2, as Helen learns how to navigate her shady job and her responsibilities as the prime minister’s wife. We also learn more about Reed (Sarah Lancashire), who works as Helen’s handler in the Black Doves spy organization. It turns out that her daughter is Helen’s nanny. Meanwhile, a new criminal outfit named Kestral plans to assassinate the prime minister and blame the killing on Helen and the Doves.

But at the end of season 2, Helen is forced to reveal her double life to her husband, who is about to find out just how much information he’s unknowingly passed on to her buyers over their years together. However, his response will likely set up season 3, as the cliff-hanger leaves audiences right before Helen begins telling him the truth about their relationship.

As of now, Netflix has yet to renew the spy thriller for a third season. That’s only natural. The second season just aired on the streamer. But according to creator Joe Barton, the writers room is already putting together potential ideas for season 3.

“Netflix are really behind it,” he told The Sun earlier this week. “They’ve said that thing, ‘We’d love to recommission it’—I’m like, No one’s stopping you, you can!”

Hopefully, another two years won’t pass before we find our answer.

#6852. An Everyman’s Guide to Wearing a Necklace

Every product was carefully curated by an Esquire editor. We may earn a commission from these links. Here’s how we test products and why you should trust us.

You already have a watch you like. This is the next step in your jewelry journey.

Men’s jewelry, I’ve learned, can be a slippery slope. I’ve been a watch guy since elementary school, if we’re generous enough to count a dual-sided compass/watch on a carabiner as a watch. In college I added a bracelet. I’ve been a ring guy for over ten years, thanks mostly to being married and partially to getting lunch drunk in Albuquerque, going ring shopping for my wife, and finding a sterling silver bear signet ring that I’ve worn nonstop since. I’ve had an earring for two years, thanks to a quick weekend in Miami and a well-timed Harrison Ford interview clip crossing my algorithm about getting his ear pierced in a Claire’s.

Recently, I’ve been curious about my personal final frontier of men’s jewelry—the necklace. The other listings above are all fairly low entry points, safe experiments in the world of men’s jewelry. The earring may be the exception, but this is 2026; one small silver hoop isn’t that daring, even in the Midwest. A necklace has never really been my thing. I haven’t felt the pull. That is, until this year.

For an unrelated project, I was breaking down some of the signature stylistic calling cards of Robert Redford. And there it was, across paparazzi pictures and movie stills and in memoriam roundups. In almost every photo, Redford has some kind of necklace, usually peeking from a precariously unbuttoned western shirt.

Further study of what we can safely call Hollywood’s golden age of off-duty style shows the same: McQueen and Newman and their contemporaries, swanning around on and off film, always wearing some sort of necklace or chain or pendant.

This is, of course, a common trap: to look at a famously handsome Hollywood star and think, yeah, all that’s separating me from THAT is a necklace. And sure, a good cheekbone and clavicle will get you pretty far in life. There’s no magic amulet here, nothing that will shazam you into leading-man looks. But there are a few lessons on styling from guys whose literal job it was to present themselves favorably to the world. And a few lessons on what necklaces to choose to help get there.

So, I put my professional online shopping style writing gig into overdrive, going deep into the Getty Images archives and confusing Google’s settings by repeatedly searching “Insert Hollywood Icon + shirtless” to glean some jewelry 101 tips from the professionals.

Instagram and (theoretically, since I don’t indulge) TikTok are full of maximalizing style trend chasers. Why wear one necklace when you can wear four? Why two rings when each finger could have two rings on it? Why dip your toes in the water when you can cannonball into the deep end? And sure, there’s some je ne sais quoi about just committing to something fully and completely out of the gate. But there’s also a lot of try-hard to it.

We’re channeling a more reserved, less #sponsoredpost era of dressing here that cares less about link clicks and more about how things look in the real world. So start simple and start with a chain. My favorite, and currently on daily rotation, is the Curb Chain from L.A.-based Bloedstone. Mine is sterling silver and in the inch length, which hits closer to the sternum than the neck. That’s the prescribed Hollywood A-lister way to wear it, but chart your own path if you want to. Miansai has a thicker 2mm Cuban chain that’s great too. And while we’re covering the M’s, Mejuri has one too. To my slight surprise, my home state watchmaker Shinola makes one, and less surprisingly so, Esquire-approved David Yurman has this giant one featuring a marketing campaign with Michael B. Jordan, who is picking up McQueen’s (and subsequently Brosnan’s) torch by adapting The Thomas Crown Affair.

There’s a whole vocabulary on link types and thickness and clasps out there. Don’t worry about that for now. Find something that calls to you and click add to cart. We’re starting slowly here.

Parting note. There are a lot of chains worn over T-shirts these days. To each their own, but the leading man’s move is to keep it under your shirt. If you want to show it off, just ditch the buttons.

A chain is simple, and sure, the greats wore them. But more often than not, they had something dangling from that chain. Medallion, pendant, a bottle opener in Cool Hand Luke. McQueen was often photographed, including in the pages of Esquire, wearing a St. Christopher medallion. Seeing as he’s the patron saint of travelers, St. Christopher medallions are having a bit of a cultural resurgence, partially because of their traditional association as a good-luck charm for travelers. There are some fun enamel ones on eBay, including these surfing-specific ones. Every once in a while, Nashville-based Americana experts Imogene + Willie will pull together a vintage edit of St. Christopher medallions that always sell out in around 24 hours. Speaking of Nashville, if you’re going to go new, go with Yearly Co. The gold jewelry experts have a 14k version of the iconography with a pitch-perfect 24-inch chain. I can attest to the quality—I gave my wife the brand’s diamond huggies and she wears them almost every day. As the grandson of a Protestant minister, I steer away from the saints out of genetic loyalty to Luther’s 95 Theses, but I recently picked up this Perseverance medallion from the brand, inspired by a vintage signet ring. It scratches the McQueen itch with flying colors.

Secondhand gold is also an option. Alloy Market recently came onto my radar, and I’m browsing it daily for myself and gifts for my wife. They’ve got a small but mighty collection of certified men’s items with pendants and medallions you can mix and match. All of the quality without any of the markup.

Don’t limit yourself to just a medallion, though. Get a little funky. Redford did for a while with this turquoise number that somehow looked even cooler hitting under the sternum. Shinola’s got an option there too. Bali-based Salty Dagger has an Odysseus-approved Greek mythology piece. And why not try a locket, like this one from Pattaraphan. Miansai has a great pendant. Get fancy with the Prevaut diamond ring deal. When in doubt, steal from the girls. I got this With Clarity birthstone necklace for my wife that I might take a swing at myself.

Peyote Bird High Desert Sterling Silver Necklace

Shinola 21mm Turquoise Inlay Tag Necklace

From the abbreviated/slightly bastardized Shakespeare: “All the world’s a stage and one man in his time plays many parts.” Jewelry can feel like a risk, even if you’re following some sort of contrived guide to styling and buying it. Sometimes we pretend until we’re comfortable actually being. Redford and McQueen and company were actors. Pretending was their legacy, and they were good at it. Take a leaf from their book and get dressed for the curtain call.

#6850. Pastel Hues and Big Jewelry: Decoding The Gilded Age Season 4’s Fashion

The new season of The Gilded Age uses fashion as a powerful storytelling method.

Everyone’s favorite HBO period drama about New York high society at the turn of the 20th century is back for a fourth season. In The Gilded Age, all the main characters (played by Carrie Coon, Christine Baranski, Audra McDonald, Cynthia Nixon, and Morgan Spector) are back. But this time, their outfits are just a little bit different. As old and new money continue to clash, the gowns, jewelry, and glamour speak louder than ever before. The outfits also show where the characters are mentally, more than ever. Within the first episode, we’ve already seen marriage, birth, and daring tensions, all dramatically dressed and detailed.

For the series, costume designer Kasia Walicka-Maimone takes inspiration from the real changing fashion of New York City from the 1870s to the 1890s: a time when trends and silhouettes were rapidly evolving. Walicka-Maimone and her team look to paintings, photography, and fashion plates from the period to inform the grand gowns and refined suiting. “We are seeing more artistic license in the dress designs this season, with traditional elements mixed with modern ones like the sleeveless top Marian wore to the after-wedding party downtown at Webster Hall,” Elizabeth L. Block, author of the Gilded Age Fashion book and newsletter, tells ELLE. “The juxtapositions are fun, maybe even more so than the one-to-one matchups with actual Gilded Age dresses we saw in the earlier seasons.”

Even if we’re early in the season, it’s fascinating to see color tell such a story through clothing. Socialite sisters Agnes van Rhijn (Christine Baranski) and Ada (Cynthia Nixon) are at the center of the show, and in the new season, their looks reflect a slightly more joyful representation of their characters. Think: embroidered details and luscious hues. “Aunt Ada is loosening up,” adds Block. “She is fully out of mourning for her husband, and we are seeing her in lighter color combinations like pink and green. For a while last season she was all buttoned up in black and deep blues.” Gleaming buttons and lace trims allude to the fact that these sisters have access to the best of the best textiles.

On the same wavelength, Peggy (Denée Benton) and her mother, Mrs. Scott (Audra McDonald), demonstrate through their clothing that they have money, but most importantly, taste. There’s a short conversation about Brussels bobbin lace that is quite revealing, however. (Consuelo Vanderbilt famously wore a Brussels lace veil for her glorious 1895 wedding to the Duke of Marlborough.) Their highly ornate outfits with richly detailed trims and embellishments are unrivaled.

Still, sisters Agnes and Ada are more toned down than someone like Bertha Russell (Carrie Coon) and her railroad tycoon husband George Russell (Morgan Spector) or Peggy and her family, who have all always used clothing as armor and a communication tool. Despite seeing Bertha dressed down early in the episode during Gladys’s (Taissa Farmiga) giving birth, she later comes to fruition with diamond tiaras, puffed and beaded sleeves, and embellished full-skirted ball gowns.

A major fashion moment comes when Enid Winterton (Kelley Curran) and Oscar van Rhijn (Blake Ritson) get married. Enid wears an opulent gown embroidered with flowers in a soft shade of pinkish lavender, with matching gloves and an ornate pink floral headpiece to match. As Block says, it’s a “pinky-lavender dress for a lavender marriage,” and “The ensemble immediately reads as incongruous but elegant and playful, like the two characters, who are now fan favorites.” With a flash of pale green and a long train, the look is a nod to the stereotype of the idea of new money being flashier than old money. Enid’s wedding look is the equivalent of a fashion debut for her in a way, and later on, we see her in a pink silk trimmed with sumptuous fur, accented with a pearl necklace and earrings.

We also see Marian Brook (Louisa Jacobson) emerge even more as an example of a young woman who’s interested in dressing differently. Her vivid mint green and black striped gown with draped details was incredibly visually striking and felt new and bold, while her matching hat felt like a nod to the kind of more mature, old-money style of her aunts. She also wears a blue lace gown with velvet shoulder details and matching opera gloves, revealing more skin than the old-money characters in the show.

If you’re a jewelry (or accessories) lover, it’s the season to watch. Enid’s spectacular diamond necklace and whimsical approach to hats covered in bows and feathers are gasp-worthy and definitely among the most entertaining parts of the show. In The Gilded Age season 4, the fashion is vital to the drama.

#6846. 27 Thoughtful Family Christmas Gifts Everyone Will Be Excited to Unwrap

Every item on this page was hand-picked by a House Beautiful editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

You’re sure to find a winner or two from our carefully curated list.

Buying family Christmas gifts can be more difficult than you think, especially if you’re shopping for an uncle you only see occasionally or the picky cousin who seems to dislike everything. The best place to start is usually to ask those closest to you for ideas, but if the suggestions from others are slow going, you can check out our curated picks ahead.

How did we select them? Well, we asked our editors for the best items they’ve ever received (or given) from their families and kept in mind all the different interests and budgets one might have while looking for gifts.

We found items that appeal to the bird watcher in the family, the sentimentalist, the design lover, and more. The 20+ items range from crowd-pleasers like a heated blanket to hyper-specific items like a stone bathmat for the germaphobes in the family. You can find products across all price points, too, because we know you may want to spend as little as $50 on someone—just know that gifts at this price point still feel thoughtful and look nice—or a couple of hundred on your favorite sibling.

Ahead, shop our top picks for the whole family.

This portable marble lamp only weighs two pounds and adds the most beautiful ambient light to their space. It has three adjustable brightness levels, and the light will gently flash to warn you when the battery is running low. Family members of all ages will appreciate this beauty, from the aunt who wants to display it on her bookshelf to the teenager going off to college who needs to decorate their dorm room to the parent who wants a chic nightlight in their nursery.

If 2027 is their year to get in touch with nature more or pick up a hobby, gift them this smart solar-powered bird feeder to encourage their newfound passion. The bird feeder has both day and nighttime vision, and when paired with a Featherpal subscription, it can identify over 10,000 bird species. However, a subscription is not needed just to see what birds visit the property.

The best games allow you to team up and tackle a challenge together. See who in your family thinks alike with Wavelength and add a prize at the end to make the game more competitive. “This is the group game I always bring on vacations or during the holidays,” Senior Commerce Editor Marina Liao says. “The rules are easy to learn, though coming up with the clue can be difficult depending on who you’re playing with and how they think! I like that everyone gets a turn, and if you happen to have very opinionated friends and family, Wavelength will get heated!”

Before you worry that this only comes as a family of three, the bear family can be personalized with up to seven pieces! The writing is laser-engraved, so the text will never fade. Display this adorable decor on a mantel, console table, bookshelf, or even on the windowsill.

Everyone could use an eye massager, especially with how much we spend looking at screens. “There was a period last year where I kept getting dry eyes, so my optometrist recommended heating pads,” Liao says. “I bought this after seeing how many reviews it had on Amazon, and it wasn’t super expensive. I used it two to three times a week for only a month and saw a dramatic improvement in my eye moisture! This massager also has tiny speakers that connect to your Bluetooth so you can listen to a podcast or music while your eyes are closed.”

Tonies were designed for the kids in the family, but everyone can enjoy the audio and storytelling. This is for the parents who don’t want to introduce tablet time too soon for their kids. Unwind at night or in the middle of a day with stories and music from the different collectibles that range from Bluey to Disney characters.

Are you still looking for a stocking stuffer? Allow us to introduce you to the Rabbit, which will make opening a bottle of wine the easiest thing you've ever done. "I've tried your traditional corkscrew wine opener, the automatic kind, and the Rabbit, and nothing compares to the Rabbit," Liao says. "All you have to do is put this over the bottle's neck and then lift the gray lever to draw the cork out of the bottle. I don't have to worry about the cork splintering, which happens whenever I use any other method, and I no longer look like a fool struggling to open wine at parties. I got the Rabbit as a gift a few years ago, and it's one of my favorite items I have received."

Does your family visit Aspen every winter? If yes, this candle set is perfect for mom, dad, sister, or even brother, as it'll help conjure up all those warm and fuzzy family memories on the mountain. Let the notes of fir needles, blue spruce, and fireplace ignite their olfactory senses.

Getting a weekly massage may not be in the cards for their schedule or budget, which is why we love an at-home massager. This device has eight different massage nodes and three adjustable speeds (slow, medium, fast). It even heats up to ease muscle tension and stress while improving blood circulation. Best of all, they can use this while watching their favorite show or on the couch while watching the grandkids play.

They don't need a spacious backyard to start growing their own herbs and veggies: just gift them the popular Click & Grow, which can be left out on their kitchen island or countertop. The smart garden uses an LED grow light and pre-seeded plant pods to give you a bountiful harvest of basil, peppers, rosemary, and more.

We'll never say no to another throw or blanket, especially if it's heated. Don't knock it until you've tried it, because the feeling of being under one after you just walked the dog in 10-degree weather, or after you just got back from a long day outside in the snow, is the best feeling in the world. This one comes in so many colors and sizes and has six different heat levels!

Do you have a creative family member or someone who likes to doodle as a hobby? If so, they will appreciate this blank canvas they can draw on using just water. Here's how it works: dip the brush in water, draw whatever you want on the surface of this board, then watch it disappear over time as the water evaporates. We love a no-mess art activity.

You may not want your little niece or baby cousin playing with your expensive camera or iPhone, but if they show interest in documenting the sweet moments at family gatherings, get them their very own kid-friendly camera. This one takes photos up to 8 megapixels and includes a 32GB memory card that can hold up to 4,000 pictures. With a fully charged battery, the camera can take 1,000 pictures or record two hours of video, giving the little ones in the family plenty of time to capture every detail.

Who doesn't love getting out of the shower or tub and being wrapped up in a toasty towel? This smart bathroom gadget will keep your towels heated for about an hour and can hold approximately two towels depending on how big they are. You can even stick your robe or clothes in there, should you want to toast those items up.

Cozy Earth consistently tops our editors' lists for the best bamboo sheets (the brand's pajamas are so comfy, too), so if you know your family members would appreciate new bedding, this set makes the perfect gift. "Every season, my husband's family does a white elephant gift exchange,” Liao says. "I've learned, over the years, they all love functional or edible gifts versus wacky ones—everyone fought over a trash can last Christmas—so I'm showing up with a set of crisp, cooling sheets in a size queen! Whether they want this for themselves or their guest rooms, I know the bougie sheets will be a hit with the practical aunts and uncles."

When there are four or more schedules to juggle in a household, it can feel overwhelming, which is why we're big proponents of a digital calendar that keeps things organized. This one is extremely popular and one of the more stylish options available.

We love Framebridge's selection of photo ornaments, and this is the type of gift that works for any family member who's putting up a tree. Whether you gift this to your aunt featuring a photo of you two or have it be a portrait of the family dog for your parents, this sentimental family gift will be precious and memorable.

Buying smart home gadgets can add up, so if you want that peace of mind without racking up your credit card bill, get a Ring Doorbell.

"This was one of the first things I bought for my front door because I live on a busy street and sometimes have random people sit on my stoop," Liao says. "The video quality is clear, even at night, and I like that you can see what else is happening around your neighborhood through the community board on the app. I feel much safer having this and being able to see who is outside my door before I open it. I've gifted a Ring Doorbell to my parents and will also gift it to my sister when she moves into a new apartment next year! I love this thing."

This kettle may be the smartest, prettiest kettle we have ever seen. It has English, French, and Spanish built in, along with a host of features you'll find helpful. You can schedule your kettle to heat to a specific temperature when you need it, choose from different preset temperatures, and customize the altitude setting depending on where you live. Additionally, there is a hold mode to keep the water hot from anywhere between 15 to 60 minutes, plus a chime to alert you that the water is done boiling. This kettle comes in four other colors if someone in your family is not so fond of blue.

Get a stone bath mat as a gift that the recipient and their whole family can appreciate. They are in for a real treat if they're not familiar with this water-wicking bath mat. "I got one years ago, and it is amazing," Liao says. "The mat dries so quickly that when it's my husband's turn to shower five minutes later, he doesn't feel any leftover wetness that lingers on a more traditional fabric bath mat. I bought one for my mother-in-law as a Christmas gift; she loved it so much that she eventually got two more. I admit this is a seemingly random gift, but once they try it out, they will never return to a plush bathmat ever again."

#6843. We’ve Tested Virtually Every At-Home Laser Hair Removal Device—These 9 Stood Out

We may earn commission from links on this page, but we only recommend products we love. Promise.

See the best picks of 2026, how they work, the results, and the deals you shouldn't miss.

Here’s my unfiltered review of laser hair removal: It’s painful, expensive, and takes a lot of sessions to see results. Soon, I'm running right back to waxing (ouch) and shaving (annoying). I thought at-home laser hair removal devices would be an expensive little beauty gadget that did nothing—yet another tool piled up next to my abandoned skincare devices. But I was so wrong. They're actually the best of both worlds.

An at-home laser hair removal device actually can help reduce the number of hairs that grow on you by damaging the follicle with every zap—all from your bed, couch, bathroom, wherever. This makes your hair look sparser, creating the illusion that you have far less hair (and making hair removal a whole lot quicker). And yep, at-home laser hair removal devices do work. They just use lower energy levels than the professional devices at a medspa or dermatologist’s office, which means they also require way more treatments to get similar results.

I’ve tried out all the top devices on the market for two months, evaluating how easy they were to use, how long they take on different areas of the body, the level of pain, and the efficacy, all to come up with this list of the top 10 out there. Here’s a peek at our top favorites.

Keep reading for a bit more info on these devices, plus a full review of all of our picks (like how we use them, the results we've seen in two months, and more).

Safety Guidelines and Skin Type Considerations:

Annoyingly, there are currently no at-home laser hair removal devices that are safe to use on dark skin and/or light hair, even if the device claims to work for “everyone.” In reality, they won’t work—or are unsafe for—any skin tones deeper than “light brown” or on hair colors lighter than “medium brown.” So make sure to speak with your dermatologist before wasting your money or, worse, damaging your skin. Got it? Good.

Now keep reading for info on how at-home laser hair removal works, the difference between IPL devices and laser devices, and first-person reviews on the best ones to try.

Why we love it: After four months of consistent testing, this Philips IPL device quickly rose in the ranks as the best laser hair removal device we’ve tried. It’s seriously high-tech, which can sometimes make something more complicated, but in this instance, it ups the beginner-friendly factor by miles. Once you connect the device to the accompanying app, the device actually speaks to you as you’re using it. So as you glide it down your leg or under your arms, the device will say if you’re doing it correctly or if you missed a spot.

Each attachment is geared toward a different body area (body—like arms and legs—face, bikini, and underarms), and they also use smart sensors to adjust the treatment to your skin’s needs, taking into account your skin tone and hair color. But the key to IPL hair removal is consistency, though, and the app actually tracks your progress and will send you a notification when you’re due for another treatment.

Cosmo editor's review: "I actually flew to Amsterdam in June to get a first sneak peek before this was available in America last month. I’ve been testing it ever since, and it has truly changed my hair removal entirely. I’m no stranger to laser hair removal devices; I’ve actually been using them on and off for six years. But this worked the fastest of anything I’ve tried. In just two treatments, spaced two weeks apart, I noticed less hair under my arms. Now, I only use it once a month or so, and my hair barely grows. I realized I have a pile of shaving creams to test, and I haven’t used a single one yet.

But the results aren’t the only thing that’s kept me consistent. I also just love how easy this is to use. Especially on areas like my bikini line, where I can’t really see what I’m doing, the device telling me that I’m doing it right—and when I’m doing it wrong—has absolutely made a difference. I only just started using this on my bikini line, as I was waiting until summer was over to avoid any potential irritation, but I’m quickly seeing some promising results. ”—BETH GILLETTE, BEAUTY EDITOR

Why we love it: A handful of Cosmo editors have tested the Ulike laser hair removal devices over the years, and every single person has shared rave reviews. And after testing five different devices on myself (doing hard work over here), I can confidently say the Air 3 model is the best one. It's affordable, extremely easy to use and set up, doesn't hurt, and comes with everything you need (including a mini razor to shave with before starting). Lemme get into it:

First of all, Ulike uses a unique "ice cooling" technology that essentially cools down your skin as it zaps you, cutting down on any pain and making your treatment really comfortable. To make it easy to use, the device has three different modes: "Soft mode" for your face and upper lip, "body mode" for your arms and legs, and "power mode" for your under arms and crotch—all of which are designed to work the best on these areas based on the thickness of skin and hair (think about it: your upper lip doesn't need the same power as your pubes). And when you actually use the tool, you can stamp it against your skin and press the button, or glide it across and it'll auto-zap you (which definitely trims treatment length).

Cosmo editor's review: "I'm no stranger to laser hair removal devices and have used a handful over the years. I really didn't think I could love one this much, though (I should have listened to my coworkers, lol). I've been putting this to use on my underarms where my skin is sensitive and gets irritated so easily. And I've never noticed any issues. Best of all, though, it's so easy to use that I've actually remained consistent. I am quick to stop doing things once they become complicated (I'm a Sagittarius! I can't help it!), but all I have to do is shave, plug this in, turn it on, and start zappin'. There aren't any useless buttons to press or apps to connect to. And the key to getting the results you want—i.e. fewer hairs over time—is keeping up with your treatments. I've used this now for two months, and I definitely am picking up the razor less. Now, I pretty much only shave when I'm going to do a treatment."—BG

Why we love it: Like the Dyson of laser hair removal devices, the Braun Skin i-Expert won the Cosmo Holy Grail Beauty Award in2024. The device pairs with a free app to take you through the whole process, so it's fantastic if you're totally new to this whole thing and need some guided help. The app also keeps track of all of your treatments so you know how often you're using it to really nab your results. There are also two methods based on different areas of your skin: A stamping method that's great for getting more precise areas, and a gliding method that you can use on your legs or underarms.

It comes with a lot (which certainly helps make up for the price). There are four heads (two precision caps for face and your bikini line, one wide cap for your body, and one standard size, all of which have skin tone and hair color sensors to avoid any potential skin damage), plus a Gillette Venus razor—aka a very good one—to shave with beforehand and a chic carrying case to store everything in.

FWIW, this Braun device is highly loved on Reddit, especially by users with tan to medium skin tones who normally find they can’t use most IPL devices without damaging their skin. One reviewer said they love that the device automatically adjusts the settings based on their skin tone, which tends to be on the low side for their medium skin. They said they used it twice weekly for five months and noticed that they barely have any hair on their underarms, legs, and bikini line these days, and even the hair that does grow comes back very slowly. So while, yes, it’s an investment, it’s a whole lot more ~fancy~ than the others on this list—and still a fraction of what you’d spend on laser hair removal treatments in-office, FYI.

One Cosmo editor's review: "I was a laser hair removal virgin, except when I tried getting my under-arms professionally lasered in high school, but my pain tolerance was too low to do more than two sessions, so I was super excited to try an at-home laser device. I loathe shaving, so I'll usually use an epilator or wax my underarms. I will say upon first impression, I loved how Braun's device came with allll the bells and whistles—including a razor. The case itself is very compact, which I also appreciated as a beauty editor with tons of tools living in a small NYC apartment. After setting up the app for about 10 minutes, the rest of the process was seamless. The device is super techy and does the adjusting for you, so all I had to do was hold the device on my skin and wait for it to flash. It wasn't completely painless, but it hurt less than my professional appointment, and a lot less than an epilator. It's safe to say that I'm officially an at-home laser convert."

Another Cosmo editor's review: "Per my testing, this device is fully the most high-tech that I’ve ever used. I connected it with the app to track my progress, which definitely has helped keep me consistent (the most pivotal point of at-home laser-hair removal that I often struggle with as a busy person). The reminders on my phone really held me accountable. The app also guided me through treatments that felt pretty quick, which made me way more likely to do them. And I especially love that I can just stuff everything back in the (tbh, very chic) carrying case to hide amongst my other beauty gadgets."—BG

Why we love it: I used to get bikini waxes every month. Now, I just shave once a week and follow up with this at-home device that leaves me smooth for a fraction of what I was spending before. This at-home laser utilizes intense pulsed light (IPL) to help gradually reduce hair growth, and I’ve noticed a significant difference, especially on my underarms and legs.

I recently told one of my friends to start with this device when she was unsure about at-home laser hair removal because it’s fairly simple and beginner-friendly. It’s got three treatment modes depending on the area you’re focusing on (gentle, speed, and power mode), 10 intensity settings, and a skin sensor so the device only flashes when it’s pressed up against a safe skin tone. The device also comes with an adjustable head plus a four-point contact system, so you really avoid missing spots (something I’ve noticed with other bulky devices). It’s been essentially foolproof for me, all while actually giving me hair-free results after three to four months.

One Cosmo editor's review: “Compared to every other IPL device I’ve tried, this is definitely the gentlest while still providing a damn good result. TBH, my legs have never been smoother—even months after finishing my last treatment.” —BG

Why we love it: Listen, I wouldn’t say at-home laser hair removal is horribly painful, but it’s definitely not comfortable. So if you’re a baby like me or have sensitive skin, try Ulike’s IPL laser-hair removal tool, which emits a cooling effect as the device passes over your skin to help reduce some pain and heat. Plus, it has five intensity levels depending on the area you’re treating, which helps cut down on unnecessary discomfort (because I def don’t need the same strong laser on my lil chin hairs as I do my legs).

Cosmo beauty contributor Mary Honkus tested this device for a full month before giving a glowing Ulike review. “If I had known how easy and effective the Ulike Air 3 was, I probably wouldn’t have spent my hard-earned cash to get my armpits professionally lasered,” she wrote. “The device has completely simplified my hair removal routine, and I know it will save me a ton of money in the long run.”

One Cosmo editor says: “My sensitive skin is prone to razor burn, so I turned to this Ulike device for a more long-term hair removal solution that wouldn’t cause as much irritation. When they say quick and painless, they actually mean it. There was no zapping or burning sensations, unlike other devices I’ve tried, and I began seeing less hair growth in a matter of weeks. Months after adding this to my routine, my underarms have never been happier.” —SARAH MABERRY, FASHION AND LUXURY COMMERCE EDITOR

Why we love it: Listen, Braun simply makes some of the best at-home laser hair removal devices. If you don’t need all the bells and whistles of the newer model, try this one, which boasts just as much intensity. It’s got 10 different modes you can toggle between, depending on the area you’re treating—and it also works so quickly. Truly, I was able to treat both of my full legs—calves and thighs—in under eight minutes, which was absolutely the fastest of any other hair-removal device I tried. Plus, it’s equipped with 300,000 flashes of light, which is the equivalent of 22 years of full-body treatments, meaning it won’t die on you mid-treatment.

Why we love it: This at-home laser hair removal device is not only seriously good at reducing hair, but it also has a “skin rejuvenation” mode that works at a lower frequency to help boost collagen and trigger elastin production. Just shave (or grab a dermaplaner for your chin or forehead), pass the tool on the face mode over your skin to help reduce hair, then turn on the SR function and glide it over your skin—avoiding your sensitive under-eyes—one to two times a week to slowly treat your skin (think softening forehead wrinkles and smoothing uneven skin texture).

Why we love it: No surprise here: Nood makes the best device to use on your bikini line, crotch, pubes—whatever you wanna call it. The Flasher Pro is their newest and best device, per our testing. They actually say it's the "most powerful at-home IPL device" on the market, and on the surface, it definitely has the specs. At 7 J/cm2, it's the strongest device on this list—but don't take that to mean it hurts. Next to the treatment window is a metal piece that stays uber cold, helping to immediately counteract the heat of the zap against your skin.

Sure, it's strong—but what's so special about this device is the shape and size. It makes treating between your legs so easy, compared to so many other devices on the market. You do have to press the button as you move the device through the treatment, but it's ergonomic enough that it's not a pain.

One Cosmo editor's review: "I was skeptical before I tried this—I'm pretty loyal to all of my other hair-removal methods for my Brazillian. But I've officially been converted with the Nood Flasher Pro. I love how easy it is to use—just turn it on and start zapping. It really doesn't hurt, thanks to the cooling metal piece, which is exactly why I was so afraid of trying a device like this on such a fragile area of skin. But rejoice, if you are like me and have sensitive skin: This did not irritate me at all—and I do a full Brazillian with it once or twice a week."—BG

Why we love it: Look, most laser hair removal devices aren't the easiest to store. They're bulky and usually come with extra-long and heavy cords that take up mega space. I could absolutely never travel with many of the other options on this list (even though I love them, ofc). But this pick from Foreo is basically made for those of us with minimal storage space. The device itself, sure, it's on the larger side, but it packs easily in a bag.

However, all of this doesn't mean the tool skimps on efficacy. The circular treatment window on this is massive compared to many others we've looked at. This means it'll take likely half as long to cover large areas of your skin, like your legs or arms. And the head adjusts and moves around so you can maneuver it more easily around small areas, like your underarms or bikini line. Once you connect the device to the app, you also get more guidance and setting options.

One Cosmo editor's review: "Okay, so bringing this home recently, my dad did think I was pulling something funky out of my bag, lol. But! It's genuinely the most compact device since the cord is a normal length. It really doesn't take up any space in my bag. I could see myself bringing this on long trips when I don't want to miss a session, or just to fit inside my teeny-tiny bathroom. And it works as effectively as many of the others I've tested."—BG

We’ve been testing at-home laser hair removal devices for five years, bringing you the best ones with all of our firsthand experience and updating whenever we try new launches or underrated gems. To compile this full list, we:

Laser hair removal is a process where specific wavelengths of light are directed onto your skin in little pulses, targeting and heating up the hair follicle to destroy a portion of it with each treatment, says dermatologist Arash Akhavan, MD. Compared to in-office treatments (which, although pricey, are done by board-certified derms or trained professionals who know exactly what they’re doing), at-home devices have a much lower energy output—mostly because they often use IPL (intense pulsed light) rather than true laser technology—which makes them safer for you to use on your own, says dermatologist Julie Russak, MD.

Yes, at-home laser-hair removal devices do work, but they take consistency. Because at-home devices use lower energy levels than in-office treatments, they require continued use (think: weekly or every time you shave) to notice similar results, says cosmetic doctor Ana Mansouri, MD. Basically, they are not for the lazy.

No, laser hair removal isn’t necessarily permanent (even though that’s what they told us). Despite how they sound, these devices don’t permanently remove hair in a few sessions, leaving you hairless like a full-body wax. Instead, laser-removal devices only help to reduce the total number of hair follicles in your skin and potentially make your existing hair finer and thinner (only electrolysis hair removal can permanently remove all hair, FYI). Even in-office laser hair removal isn’t completely permanent. Typically, you’ll need to go in once every 8 to 12 weeks after you’ve done your round of treatments (which is usually between 6 to 12, depending on the area, your hair, etc.)

Neither IPL nor laser-hair removal is “better”—it really just comes down to preference. True laser hair removal only uses one wavelength of light (essentially, one precise laser beam) that targets just the hair follicle to help slow down hair growth. IPL (intense pulsed light), on the other hand, isn’t actually a laser. Instead, they emit broad-spectrum light in multiple wavelengths that spread across a larger area of skin, meaning they are less precise and won’t penetrate your skin as deeply. That’s why IPL devices are generally gentler and easier for people to use, which is why most at-home devices use IPL rather than laser beams.

That said, both IPL and laser-hair removal can slowly destroy your hair follicle to reduce hair growth over time with continued use. But expect laser-hair removal to be a bit stronger (and potentially more painful or irritating), which is why it often yields quicker and better results. Meanwhile, IPL devices are usually not as intense, so they’re great for using consistently at home or for use on sensitive skin, like on your bikini line or face.

Do dermatologists recommend at-home laser hair removal?

Yes, it’s okay to do laser-hair removal at home, according to Dr. Akhavan, but there are some things to consider. “At-home devices tend to be generally safe, though a real potential for adverse effects, like scarring, does exist,” he says. Which is why most dermatologists will suggest opting for the professional in-office route, if you have the means (laser hair removal can cost anywhere from $200 to $1,500 and usually requires at least six sessions spaced six weeks apart).

Just note: “If you’re using an at-home device, don’t use it on sensitive areas, like your face and neck,” says Dr. Akhavan. “And if you have sensitive skin, always patch-test first on a smaller area, then wait three to four weeks to make sure there are no complications.” And depending on the area you’re treating, you may also need to adjust your skincare routine to exclude skin-thinning ingredients (like chemical exfoliants or retinol serums) for three days before and after your laser-hair removal treatment.

Does at-home laser hair removal work on dark skin?

Currently, at-home laser-hair removal devices don’t truly work for dark skin. These lasers work by targeting the dark color of your hair follicle, and at-home devices don’t have the technology yet to properly distinguish between dark hair follicles and dark skin, meaning they can potentially burn you. While some devices might market themselves as being safe for dark skin, they are usually considering medium-to-tan skin versus actual deep-brown skin tones.

So far, there are no at-home devices that are safe to use on true type-six Fitzpatrick scale skin tones (reminder: This dermatological scale ranges from one to six, with six being “brown to dark-brown” skin). Most laser-hair removal devices are only approved for up to level-four skin tones, with four being “olive to medium” skin. But if you’re unsure where your skin tone lies, talk to your dermatologist before you try an at-home laser device.

What happens if you don’t shave before at home laser hair removal?

Yes, you should shave about 24 hours before using an at-home laser-hair removal device, otherwise the IPL/laser won’t be able to correctly target the melanin (pigment) in your hair follicle. This could potentially cause discomfort, like redness, swelling, and irritation. Because these devices work by homing in on dark, contrasting colors (think: a black dot on a white canvas), they need to be able to differentiate between your skin and your follicle to prevent errors or burns. FYI: Even stubble isn't okay for laser hair removal because it will create too much heat and can damage your skin (plus, it won’t even work to help reduce the hair anyway).

Just remember: Don’t wax before your laser hair removal. Waxing completely rips out the hair and its root, which will leave nothing for the light to target, and you won’t be able to use your device. Instead, make sure your skin is freshly shaved and free of lotions or creams.

At-home laser hair removal can be slightly painful for some, but it all depends on your pain tolerance. Many people describe it as a light sting—like a rubber band snapping against your skin—but some people don’t even notice any pain at all. Your device’s strength and intensity levels will also dictate how painful the treatment will be. In general, though, most people say it’s relatively comfortable when done at home (I would give it a 1 out of 10—it’s a piece of cake, IMO).

For the most part, yes, you can use at-home laser hair removal devices on your bikini line. But you should be very careful. This should only ever be done externally on your vulva. And keep in mind how sensitive the skin in your pubic region is. Generally, it's best to opt for the lightest setting, and go slow with the device. Of all of the at-home IPL devices we tested, our favorite for pubic hair was the NOOD Flasher Pro.

It's best to skip lasering until your skin has cleared if you're dealing with razor bumps. Reminder: Razor bumps are the tiny red bumps you get on your skin after shaving or waxing when the hair strand grows back into the skin instead of out. They're usually inflamed and irritated, which is why it's ideal to just let them heal and swipe on a soothing treatment for a few days before lasering.

If you’re just starting out with at-home laser hair removal, there can be a slight learning curve. Keep these in mind:

Like I said above, you have to shave beforehand to see any reduction in hair, and it’s usually recommended to shave right before. Usually, I’ll exfoliate in the shower the day before with a body scrub, then 24 hours later, I’ll shave and use my laser-hair removal device on clean, dry skin. Exfoliating the day before helps cut down on some irritation but still ensures a close shave.

While laser hair removal is typically well-tolerated, it can potentially make your skin a little inflamed and irritated. To offset this, always finish your treatments with a moisturizing body treatment, whether that’s a body lotion, body serum, or rich body butter. And if you’re prone to ingrown hairs, try incorporating an exfoliating treatment once or twice a week, like a chemical exfoliant pad or serum.

Remember: Laser hair removal takes time. One treatment won’t do much, and neither will a couple. It takes up to three months to start noticing a reduction in hair. Stay consistent (this usually means treating your skin once a week, but it depends on your skin type).

Only some devices are suitable for deep skin tones, and even fewer can work on light hair, so read the description of the product carefully, then scan the reviews for people who have a similar skin tone or hair color as you and see how they rate the device. We noted above if a device can be used on lighter hair, fyi.

You’ll also want to consider the size of the device you’re purchasing and the area that you intend to use it on, says Dr. Mansouri. Basically, a tiny device meant for your face probably isn’t going to be the best if you’re looking for a tool to quickly target your legs.

Do you want a device you can take on the go? Then you should definitely opt for something cordless (The only one we tested that we loved was by Tria Beauty, FYI). Or if you want something that’s going to be really easy to use, try the Braun Skin-I Expert, which connects to an app to help you track your treatments. Another loved feature by testers? A cooling effect to help bring down potential discomfort and pain, like the Ulike IPL device.

Beth Gillette is the beauty editor at Cosmopolitan and has more than eight years of experience writing skincare stories, like bikini trimmers and hair-removal creams. To compile this list, she interviewed dermatologists, scoured Amazon reviews, and tested at-home laser-hair removal devices.

She can generally be found in bright eyeshadow furiously typing her latest feature or hemming and hawing about a new product you "have to try." Prior to Cosmopolitan, she wrote and edited beauty content as an Editor at The Everygirl for four years. Follow her on Instagram for makeup selfies and a new hair 'do every few months.

#6839. How Club Kid Fashion Went From the Dance Floor to the Runway

The underground scene’s DIY, gender-bending style still shapes how we get dressed today.

For his fall/winter 2009 runway show, “The Horn of Plenty,” Alexander McQueen offered a satirical critique of fashion’s throwaway culture. Models navigated a runway strewn with glass and discarded props in houndstooth looks and silhouettes that mocked fashion’s excess. Their alabaster-white painted faces and exaggerated lips evoked Leigh Bowery, the Australian performance artist known for his audacious club looks. “It’s a sackable offense, this collection,” McQueen said post-show. “I want people to look at it and say, ‘What the hell is that?’”

Much like McQueen upended fashion with his confrontational approach to design, Club Kids—a name given to the scene’s most flamboyant clubgoers, Bowery included—did the same in cities like New York and London. The scene was rife with larger-than-life, sometimes debaucherous personalities expressing themselves through equally outsized clothes; no look was too outlandish, no party too wild. It was that DIY spirit, championed by the likes of Susanne Bartsch, a nightlife impresario, RuPaul, and the infamous Michael Alig, that caught on beyond the clubs, creating an inextricable connection between nightlife and fashion. “You didn’t have to wait for a designer or a magazine to tell you what was fashionable,” Bartsch tells ELLE. “You could create a look, walk into the room, and see what happened. The crowd became the show, and the dance floor became a runway with no fixed rules.”

“Susanne, when she moved to New York, she opened a boutique and was the first person to carry clothes by [John] Galliano and [Jean Paul] Gaultier, [really] introducing that type of style into the city,” explains Ryan Burke, a New York-based makeup artist. “And then she also threw these parties; it went really hand in hand.”

Bartsch’s legendary parties at Savage and the Copacabana brought together a true amalgamation of worlds, from downtown denizens to fashion heavyweights like Thierry Mugler and Gaultier. (Like McQueen, Gaultier referenced Bowery in a 1991 runway show.) It was not only an intermixing of punchy, confident aesthetics, but also the idea that fashion can be an escape and the ultimate form of self-expression. My club nights in the ’80s brought together artists, designers, photographers, performers, and kids creating their own looks,” Bartsch notes. “For someone who has felt judged or excluded, that can be powerful. The [dancefloor] gives you permission to try something on not just an outfit, but a version of yourself.”

Meanwhile, in London, the Blitz Kids channeled that same appetite for theatrical self-expression through their DIY, gender-bending looks, which would influence collections by Marc Jacobs (most famously, his grunge collection for Perry Ellis), McQueen, and Anna Sui.

The AIDS crisis took an enormous toll on the communities that made New York nightlife pulse. Then came New York’s tough-on-crime crackdown, which helped drive many of the most popular clubs out of business. Today, the Club Kids’ heyday has the glow of downtown legend: a moment when self-expression ruled the dance floor and anyone could make an entrance. Now, Burke notes that social media has changed how people create and share their looks, making the heyday of the Club Kids feel all the more singular. (In film, the scene’s legacy has been in 2003’s Chloë Sevigny-starring Party Monster and is now slyly resurfacing in Jordan Firstman’s new film, Club Kid, where he plays a club promoter whose life is upended by the arrival of the 10-year-old son he never knew he had.)

“People are really crafty, really crafty online; they create, document it, take it off,” he says. “That’s cool too; any kind of way people want to express themselves is great, but there was something that was really magical about seeing people out. They tried more interesting things that might not work or might not look that good, but they tried it.”

The Club Kid spirit still reverberates in the underground scenes of New York, London, and beyond—and at the highest levels of fashion. You just need to know where to look.

During the recent spring/summer 2027 season, when many designers celebrated the “joy of getting dressed,” the club was never too far away. At Junya Watanabe, pearls and punk hardware were stacked atop catsuits with the carefree abandon of the original club kids, who built their looks from punk boutiques and thrift-store finds. Diesel got hot and heavy: Glenn Martens’s swan song for the brand unfolded amid a crowd of performers kissing and touching, while models wore barely-there denim and clothes that looked hastily thrown on, finished with smudged red lipstick, as if they’d been smooching on the dance floor. And August Barron showed a starlet-inspired lineup of glitzy “going out” dresses, sandals with neon heels, and haphazardly layered separates.

It’s easy to see why fashion keeps returning to the club: Nowhere else makes getting dressed feel quite so alive. As Bartsch puts it: “For me, the club spirit isn’t one particular look, it’s freedom, imagination and the confidence to express yourself without asking permission.”

#6835. 7 Desert Boots That Can Survive the Winter

Every product was carefully curated by an Esquire editor. We may earn a commission from these links. Here’s how we test products and why you should trust us.

Despite the name, these chukkas are built to be worn in all conditions.

Winter weather can get ugly. If it’s not wind and rain, it’s slushy sidewalks and unexpected snow flurries. You obviously need shoes that can handle a little precipitation, but the key phrase here is a little. You don’t want to stomp around in heavy winter boots, especially if we want to look nice. Dress shoes are a tough fit in winter, as are dress boots. Funny enough, between December and March, you know what our go-to footwear becomes? Desert boots. Technically chukka boots, but a few desert boots make the cut here.

But that’s something to note. The Esquire office does not use the term interchangeably—but the Internet does, so we’re going along with it. We know some of you—nerds, mostly—have stopped reading this article because you don’t think we know the difference between the two. We’re well aware of the square and rectangle-ism: All desert boots are chukkas, not all chukkas are desert boots.

If you’re not a nerd and want to learn something new, chukkas are ankle-high boots with open lacing and two or three pairs of eyelets, often made with leather uppers—leather or rubber soled. Desert boots are a subsection of this silhouette that typically features a suede upper (nubuck, sometimes) with lighter-colored, more flexible crepe soles. They are not as winterized—suede, especially, is known to take a beating from moisture—hence the name. The details vary here and there, but both styles can work for winter if you choose wisely.

We found seven pairs of chukka boots—yes, some of which are desert boots—with weather-friendly features, from water-resistant uppers to sturdy rubber soles. Most have both, so you can find a pair that looks sharp without leaving you entirely at the mercy of the winter weather forecast.

These chukka boots might as well be dress boots. They look sharp no matter what outfit you pair them with, and the ultra-refined, premium calfskin leather upper is naturally water-resistant; to a point, that is—we wouldn’t wear them in the pouring rain.

They’re very comfortable thanks to a soft, leather lining on the inside and open-cell foam insoles that provide supportive cushioning. And the flexible outsoles made from XL Extralight injection molding are a nice touch that give the boot some lightweight flexibility.

For a classic pair of chukka boots that come at a good price and have a wide range of colors and sizes, Thursday Boot Co. is the way to go. These chukkas come in a variety of colors and materials, but our favorite has to be the Mocha colorway in weather-safe suede. It’s rare to find a pair of suede shoes you can actually get wet without ruining, but these ones can brave the weather while still looking great. And with studded rubber outsoles, you have some extra traction and durability. If you want even more traction and durability in the soles, try one of the Rugged & Resilient styles with anti-slip wedge rubber outsoles.

Here’s another suede option you can actually wear during the winter; Sabah treats the suede upper of this boot to be water resistant, but you can still add a suede treatment for extra protection if you want to. These boots are handmade in Monte San Giusto, Italy, and you can trust that they were made with lots of skill and care. The insole and midsole are made from vegetable tanned leather, so they end up forming to your feet once you wear them, making them extra comfortable.

If you like the look of a gum-sole sneaker, you might like how it looks on a boot, too. With these desert boots, SeaVees blends the classic gum-sole look with the more rugged desert boot style, and the result is a versatile boot that can withstand pretty much any weather. With water-resistant rugged oiled leather uppers and natural rubber soles, these guys can get you through quite a lot.

These are going to be the least weather-ready on this list. You don’t want to take them out in a snowstorm, but damn do they look good. Imagine these worn to a holiday party, worn with a nice pair of chinos and fair-isle sweater.

The suede upper is a true not-water-resistant suede. But they do have durable rubber soles. The stitched moc-toe is a fun detail that makes these chukka boots stand out from the rest of the pack. Drake’s notes that these boots run small, so they recommend sizing up by a half-size when ordering online.

We’re starting to get pretty far away from the chukka heart, but you can see the chukka-shaped vamp and the ankle-y shape. Plus, when we think of rugged workwear boots, we think of Timberland. The upper is made from waterproof leather and has a TimberDry waterproof membrane for extra protection, and you can see that Gripstick rubber outsole gives you some distance from the ground and provides great traction as well.

And finally, we can’t talk about chukka boots without mentioning Clarks. The original Clarks desert boot was designed in 1949 and inspired by the rough suede and crepe-soled boots worn by off-duty British soldiers during WWII (as well as the shoes worn by polo players in India and South African veldskoen shoes). Today, the brand’s original style is still going strong, and you can get a pair for under $100.

#6832. Martine Rose Is the New Creative Director of Balenciaga

An appointment the fashion world is eager to celebrate

Fashion fans rejoice: Martine Rose has officially been appointed creative director of Balenciaga following yesterday’s exit of Pierpaolo Piccioli. This appointment represents a welcome departure from the circulation of familiar names for these creative director roles and symbolizes a shift back to an edgier Balenciaga established by Demna. She begins November 16.

Rose was rumored to be up for the job when it became available after Demna’s departure to Gucci in 2025. And it’s a homecoming; when Demna was appointed to Balenciaga as creative director in 2015, he brought Rose on as a menswear consultant. In her three years working there, she helped to shape the look of his very distinctive vision.

Rose was born in South London in 1980 to a British Jamaican family. Her mother was a nurse and her father was an accountant. She spent her childhood around slightly older relatives deeply immersed in ’90s rave subcultures. The symbolically rich clothing choices shaped her early aesthetic way more than any Paris runway could. She studied fashion design at Middlesex University, where she discovered an affinity with menswear. Rose began creating early, opening the small T-shirt line LMNOP with a friend in 2002. She launched her namesake label in 2007 and began showing under the umbrella of Lulu Kennedy’s fashion incubator program Fashion East in the early 2010s. That’s where she began gaining traction in niche fashion circles.

With her own collection, Rose elevated her memories of clubs—and the clashes of the different tribes within them—for a fashion audience, offering revisions of those shiny shirts, baggy pants, and anoraks. She is known for subverting archetypal garments, distorting proportions, and invoking unconventional fabrics like satin and lace. Her work nods to subcultural heroes who used fashion to convey identity, like the Lo Lifes and Dapper Dan. She can shrink a pair of pants just enough to be a little awkward and pair them with a sports jersey and loafers with ultra-extended toes in an ensemble that somehow makes total sense. Through her lens, the mundane becomes complex, thought-provoking, even extraordinary.

Demna caught on to what Rose was doing and brought her on to develop Balenciaga menswear following his appointment in 2015. She worked with him for three years and helped influence his highly recognizable men’s aesthetic, one that often featured the exaggerated shoulders, boxy cuts, and logo experimentation that she already favored. Her work at the luxury house brought attention to her own label, buoying its renown in fashion. She has since produced several high-profile collabs with brands like Nike, Supreme, and Clarks, and she counts Timothée Chalamet, Rihanna, and Hailey Bieber among her devotees.

Balenciaga is having a bit of an identity crisis. The couture house was founded by Cristóbal Balenciaga in 1917 in San Sebastián, Spain, and later reestablished in Paris in 1937. Often referred to as an “architect” of fashion rather than a designer, Cristóbal is remembered for a vision rooted in shape, volume, and silhouette. His creations were both sculptural and fluid, with iconic looks including the “tunic” and “sack” silhouettes. His legacy was carried on by Michel Goma, Alexander Wang, and most notably, Nicolas Ghesquière and Demna.

In 2025, amid an industrywide reshuffling of creative directors, Balenciaga appointed Pierpaolo Piccioli to its helm, tasking him with interpreting the house’s legacy of sculptural elegance without alienating the streetwear superfans Demna courted. It was a difficult job; Piccioli left just 16 months later. Rose’s appointment shows that the house is looking to reignite some of Demna’s subversive edge. But zooming out, her return is undeniably a celebratory one; she is beloved by fashion and streetwear fans alike. It feels in alignment with the excitement around Grace Wales Bonner’s appointment to Hermès. The current roster of creative directors at big luxury houses is mostly white and male; these are two women of color whose work has been quietly shaping the fashion landscape without always getting their due.

#6830. The Apple Watch Deals You Need to Look for This Black Friday

Every product was carefully curated by an Esquire editor. We may earn a commission from these links. Here’s how we test products and why you should trust us.

We’re expecting record-low deals in the coming weeks—but for now, we’ll take $250 off.

It’s no secret that Apple has been dominating tech headlines this year. But between the news of its recent price hikes on MacBooks and iPads and the release of the iPhone Duo (the tech giant’s first foldable), not much fanfare has been made about the new generations of the Apple Watch. As far as we’re concerned, that’s a damn shame, because they’re well worth the upgrade—especially if you can find one on sale like we just did.

Apple Watches usually go on deepest discount during Amazon sales, Black Friday included. And while only two models are marked down right now (the Ultra 4 and Ultra 3), we know a thing or two about how Apple deals work. In the coming weeks, prices will drop and these wearables will sell out like hotcakes, which is why you’ll want to plan what you’re going to buy now.

Below, we’re breaking down the differences between each model—and peeling back the curtain on our price-tracking prowess—so you’re all set come Black Friday. If you don’t take the plunge on one before then, that is.

Commerce editor Luke Guillory argued that compared to other fitness trackers on the market, Apple was lagging behind with its lack of readiness score functionality—until now. The Apple Watch Series 12 marks the debut of the brand’s very own readiness score thanks to a revamped tracking system. Plus, the watch now measures your heart rate more frequently to deliver Heart Rate Variability (HRV) readings every five minutes. If you’re trying to pay closer attention to your health this year, it’s a smart buy, made all the sweeter when it inevitably goes back on sale for Black Friday.

For October Prime Day, this brand-new watch surprisingly dropped to just $350, so we’re expecting a similar—if not deeper—discount in the coming weeks.

While the Apple Watch Ultra 4 isn’t necessarily reinventing the wheel, it did get the same advanced health tracking and readiness score features from the Apple Watch Series 12, so if you’re looking to get your first Ultra model, it’s worth grabbing—especially when it’s $100 off. Not to mention, Guillory is partial to the new ocean-inspired, semi-translucent rubber watch bands.

That said, if you’re not someone who needs the shiny new gadget immediately or who won’t take advantage of these souped-up health features—you’re not going to miss out on much if you score an older model on sale, like this $250 discount on the Apple Watch Ultra 3. Associate Commerce Editor Bryn Gelbart went so far as to dub it the “best Apple Watch ever” when it was released last fall.

“I was never tempted to upgrade to the premium option, but the Apple Watch Ultra 3 changed my mind,” Gelbart said. “It turns out I didn't quite know what I was missing.” It has a bright 49mm display, satellite messaging features, a durable titanium case, and a long lasting battery (an impressive 42 hours under normal use and 72 hours on Low Power Mode). Gelbart recommends it for cyclists, runners, or the adventure-prone.

At 28% off, this is the best pre-Black Friday deal to shop as of publication, although this model has dipped as low as $600 before.

If you’re looking for Apple’s most affordable watch, we suggest turning your attention to the entry-level Apple Watch SE 3. It was actually the watch that converted Gelbart to Apple wearables in the first place, arguing that its beauty is in its simplicity.

“It's an accurate and predictive workout tracker. It counts my steps and activity and connects to my phone to play music and receive messages and calls,” he says. “If you’re new to the Apple Watch and want to dip your toes, this is where I recommend you start.” It has the same sleep tracking features, like nightly sleep score and sleep apnea notifications, but lacks the ECG app or hypertension notifications of its newer siblings. It also has an 18-hour battery life so you’ll need to charge most nights.

This dropped to a record-low $199 during October Prime Day, so we’re hopeful that a similar price cut will emerge for Black Friday, but this is by far the most affordable Apple Watch on the market, even at full price.
