#6758. With the Hunger Games Press Tour, Have We Reached the Final Frontier of Method Dressing?

The cast has offered a pointed take on the state of today’s red carpets

Another Hunger Games movie, a prequel to the initial series, premieres later this month, and with it comes another press tour full of fantastically far-fetched fashion. As the promotional events begin to stack up for Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping, we are reminded of the familiar lore of this dystopian empire: In a fictionalized future America called Panem, the 12 districts that supply resources to the rich and powerful people of the Capitol are forced to send two children to fight to the death each year. The excess of the Capitol is signaled in the films via outlandish style, which the newest film’s cast members have been attempting to channel in their recent looks. The goal is to be extreme—but in an era of extremes on the red carpet, these over-the-top ensembles actually don’t look so out of place.

Elle Fanning plays a young Effie Trinket, who is essentially a Capitol stylist dressing the young “tributes” in all sorts of fanciful fashions—and doing the same for herself. (In the first film series, the character wore a lot of McQueen.) So far, Fanning’s press looks have deliberately channeled that outlandishness. For a London fan screening, she wore a gown from Robert Wun’s Fall 2026 couture collection that subverted ideas of childlike wonder. Her ensemble began in miniature with a music-box-style ballerina atop a bubblegum pink fascinator. The corresponding human-size gown features a doubled-up bodice, the outer layer appearing to peel off, above a full tulle skirt, all in that same dusty pink.

For her other appearances, Fanning has established a de facto uniform of precisely tailored skirt suits, each paired with some sort of coordinating fascinator tilted just so above her brow. She has selected a soft pink pleated skirt suit from Valentino complete with a ruffled collar, gloves, and a butterfly-trimmed chapeau; a sharp-shouldered version in a deep, almost reptilian satin green from Demna’s Gucci; and a floral, bow-embellished one from Vivienne Westwood. The looks are decidedly feminine in a manner that is at once both futuristic and retro in very Capitol fashion.

Fanning’s stylist Samantha McMillen has been vocal about the references to the character, with captions like “Gucci Effie | @demna puts “The Hunger” into @thehungergames,” and “Elle bringing 🦋 “Sunrise” 🦋 to the Academy Gala.” And it’s not just Fanning doing this either. Costar Mckenna Grace recently recreated a Katniss Everdeen Capitol tour look in which Katniss’s dress quite literally caught fire. Created by Vietnamese designer Cong Tri, who is known for his sculptural silhouettes, the recreation nixed the pyrotechnics but printed graphic flames onto the skirt and bodice. With the help of stylist Molly Dickson, Grace also revived Katniss’s wedding dress with a frothy white, silver-embellished gown by Monique Lhuillier.

I haven’t seen the most recent films, but all of them examine the same concept of this dystopian society propped up by the Hunger Games themselves at different points on a timeline. In the first film specifically, the older Trinket uses their version of a press tour to craft a narrative around Katniss and her fellow tribute Peeta Mellark and win favor among their audience through larger-than-life fashion. The aforementioned fire dress referenced Everdeen’s district’s coal mining industry, and the wedding dress was meant to create the illusion of a love story between the two of them. The series of looks is designed to be projected to the surrounding communities—and garner as much attention as possible. The characters can quite literally benefit later in the life-and-death-style games from the loyalties and sympathies the theatrics spawn.

It’s only in recent years that this idea of method dressing, or theming press tour looks around an actor’s current project, has become commonplace. It began in earnest with the work of Law Roach and Zendaya around the Dune and Spider-Man franchises, Challengers, and The Drama. It was perhaps commercially crystallized in 2023 by Andrew Mukamal and Margot Robbie with Barbie—a press tour that spawned so much digital attention it earned its own coffee-table book—and, more recently, Wuthering Heights. Now, it has proof of concept, attracting stars like Cynthia Erivo and Ariana Grande in their promotion of Wicked, the new cast of Sense and Sensibility, and Lili Reinhart’s rom-com references for The Love Hypothesis. At its most reductive, the tactic is a surefire way to drum up conversation on social media; at its best, a clever way to add depth to a project’s storytelling.

As press tours become more and more oriented towards social media, it’s difficult to isolate the influence of method dressing on the red carpet’s current proclivity towards extremes. Everyone is trying to capitalize on the sort of hype that the Met Gala ensembles can drum up. Your reference needs to be loud enough to cut through the noise—pyrotechnics optional. It’s perhaps why avant-garde, couture, and couture-level designers like Wun, who dressed a large handful of stars at this year’s Met Gala, are carving out more and more space among these sorts of promotional events. At the same time, brands like Standing Ground and Matieres Fecales—it’s only a matter of time before Fanning wears one of those skirt suits—are also gaining traction as stylists treat the red carpet more like a magazine editorial than an occasion to get dressed up.

Then last night, Grace added another layer. She and Dickson have begun to look outside the films to reference looks of Jennifer Lawrence’s own. Lawrence played Katniss in the first movies. For a Madrid premiere, she wore a Miss Sohee couture dress that paid homage to the Givenchy naked dress Lawrence wore for this year’s Golden Globes. It all feels very meta, calling into question the role of fashion in these promotional spaces, real or fictional. On the IRL Hunger Games red carpet, the reference is dystopian extravagance—but with the rise of method dressing and the corresponding celebration of larger, louder looks, has dystopian extravagance already become the norm? In this case, it may not be life and death, but it could make or break your movie.

#6757. I Wear-Tested En Route’s Viral, Under-$50 Jewelry—Now I Get Why My Favorite Celebs Love It

We may earn commission from links on this page, but we only recommend products we love. Promise.

Shop the pieces worn by Bella Hadid, Lola Tung, and Doechii.

What do Bella Hadid, Doechii, Camila Cabello, and Lola Tung all have in common? They’re all known for killing it on the carpet, yes—but once the cameras went down, I took notice that they’ve each been wearing the same under-$100 jewelry brand.

It might surprise you that some of the biggest stars in entertainment are wearing budget-friendly baubles. But after adding a few choice accessories from the brand to my own collection, I have to admit: En Route has some of the trendiest, most compliment-garnering jewelry the internet has to offer. (And, let’s face it: it doesn’t hurt that it costs less than the price of my favorite takeout.)

Ahead, I’m giving my honest review on En Route’s most popular pieces after months of wear-testing in my everyday jewelry rotation. Keep reading for the rundown on this viral, celebrity-loved brand—including the affordable pieces I think are worth it.

As an editor who’s been covering jewelry trends for years, I’ll admit that I was a bit skeptical when I saw the price tag. In my experience, $30 jewelry either (A) turns your skin a sickly shade of green, or (B) tarnishes to an unbecoming rust color in a matter of weeks. That’s why I wanted to put En Route’s pieces to the test. I wore them to work, regularly washed my hands with them, kept them on for sweaty outdoor runs while marathon training, and even accidentally showered in them a time or two. (Ya know, the normal wear and tear that your jewelry is going to experience throughout its lifetime.)

The brand claims its jewelry is hypoallergenic, meaning that it’s lead- and nickel-free and should be safe for shoppers with sensitive skin. Its gold-plated jewelry is also three times thicker than industry standard, according to its FAQ section, which means it’s designed to last longer than competing budget brands—a claim I was excited to put to the test.

Without spoiling my full review, here’s the TL;DR: if you want to shop trendy, unique pieces that show off your personal style, you should be running to add En Route to your collection.

Before we dive in, it’s worth noting that all of En Route’s jewelry is gold-plated—not solid gold. What does this mean? The base of the jewelry is made from an inexpensive metal, like brass or stainless steel, and then a very thin layer of gold is electroplated on top. This gives the look of real gold without the price tag.

As you might expect, gold-plated jewelry isn’t nearly as long-lasting as solid gold and silver; the thin layer will eventually rub off, particularly on jewelry like rings or bracelets that receive a lot of wear and tear. In my experience, standard gold-plated jewelry will begin fading or tarnishing within one to three years.

To ensure the longevity of your jewelry, En Route recommends avoiding water and chemicals like makeup or perfume (though showering every once in a while is A-okay)—and they even have an entire section of their site for waterproof jewelry that’s safe to get wet.

I’m not exaggerating when I say that I receive at least one compliment every time I wear one of my necklaces from En Route. Over the summer, I found myself reaching for the Infinity Choker almost every day, since its colorful beads glimmer in the sunshine and look great with a simple white tank top or sundress. These days, I’m spicing up turtlenecks and basic tees with this vintage-inspired collar necklace that looks like a family heirloom but costs less than $40.

After several months of frequent wear, both of my picks have held up without so much as a smudge. Just note that neither is advertised as being waterproof, so I’d definitely avoid wearing them in the shower or during a workout to keep them looking shiny and new for as long as possible.

Upon first glance, I was immediately impressed by how unique En Route’s ring selection is—and after testing them for a few months, I’ve become even more of a fan. The selection is basically perfect if you’re looking to shop personality-driven pieces that express your unique style. Take Bella Hadid, for example. The star was spotted doubling up with the Wonder Pearl ring on multiple fingers, showing off the chunky sculptural bezel and a pretty faux pearl inside. Or, consider Lola Tung’s stack of hammered silver rings—a master class in simple yet effective ring stacking.

I, on the other hand, found myself enamored by the Mojave Buckle ring. It runs a little bit small, but I love the subtle Western flair it adds to any look. The brand recommends keeping its rings out of water as much as possible, but even with regular hand-washing, I haven’t noticed any tarnishing or fading so far.

As someone with multiple piercings, I’m here to tell you that you can never have too many earrings. The greatest perk I found while testing En Route’s earring selection is just how lightweight they are—which is essential if you want to be comfortable all day and avoid stretching out your piercings. Despite sturdy-looking shapes and ornate details, the earrings I tested were feather-light and virtually unnoticeable all day long.

Possibly my favorite jewelry piece I tested from the brand were these Star earrings. They garnered multiple compliments from friends and strangers alike, and people were shocked when I told them they cost just $22. What’s more, the stainless steel material doesn’t irritate my ears and this pair just so happens to be waterproof.

Bella Hadid wearing the Silent Drop earrings in gold.

Lola Tung wearing the Clio earrings in silver.

My only word of caution: while the earrings look expensive, their lightweight construction makes them feel a little cheap in your hands. This isn’t a dealbreaker for me since they’ve held up flawlessly so far, but don’t expect them to have the same heft and quality of your pricey solid gold studs.

I’m not a big bracelet person. There’s something about the feeling of jewelry sliding and clanking around on my wrists that really bothers me—so it’s a rare occasion when I decide to put one on. But for the sake of this review, I tested the Athena bracelet and the Harmonic Hour watch, and honestly? I kinda loved them.

While I’m still not a fan of the clinking feeling, I loved the colored gemstone details that glittered in direct light and added a cool-girl flair with virtually zero effort. The lightweight construction makes them almost unnoticeable throughout the day, so I didn’t notice them as much as hefty bangles. Bonus points for the fact that they’re pretty easy to put on and take off by yourself, since they have simple clasps and T-bar closures. There’s even body jewelry and hand chains for more ways to personalize your jewelry stack.

After several months of constant wear-testing, I’m convinced: En Route is one of the best affordable jewelry brands on the market if you’re looking for cute, trendy, and personality-driven pieces. The wide selection of options—ranging from chunky statement pieces to wearable basics in both gold and silver—makes it super easy to express your personal style without dropping hundreds of dollars.

For shoppers with sensitive skin, I love that everything is hypoallergenic, according to the brand, so you don’t have to worry as much about how your skin will react to your new affordable jewelry. And while not everything is designed to hold up in water, I love that there’s a dedicated section on the website for shopping waterproof pieces. Even the rings, earrings, and necklaces I tested held up well with occasional splashes and frequent hand-washing.

En Route’s overall quality for the price is one of the best I’ve seen. That said, if you’re looking for investment-worthy jewelry you can wear literally 24/7—as in, at the gym, in the shower, or to sleep—I’d recommend investing in a longer-lasting (albeit more expensive) premium metal option. Nearly everything onsite is gold- or rhodium-plated, so they’ll likely start tarnishing within a couple of years, unlike pricier vermeil or solid gold and silver pieces.

Samantha Jones is a senior shopping editor at Hearst Magazines, where she specializes in style, wellness, and home content. She has more than 8 years of editorial experience, with bylines across ELLE, Cosmopolitan, Esquire, Good Housekeeping, Better Homes & Gardens, PEOPLE, Real Simple, and more. At the office, Samantha can often be found reporting on emerging style trends, curating the perfect 5-minute makeup routine, or wear-testing the latest running shoe launches for a story. She’s also an avid runner, repeat marathoner, and former Division I athlete. (In fact, when she’s not at her desk, she’s probably out for a run.)

#6755. 22 Designer Handbags That Will Stand the Test of Time

Few fashion purchases carry as much weight, both literally and financially, as a designer handbag. The right one can make an outfit, become a daily fixture on morning commutes, and, in some cases, retain its value long after checkout. But in a market where a new It bag seems to emerge every season (or with every scroll through your feed), figuring out which styles are worth the splurge isn't always straightforward.

Fashion history offers clues to sound investments. Some of today’s most coveted bags have been around for decades: Gucci’s Jackie traces its roots to the 1960s, while Dior’s Lady Dior became an icon of ’90s style thanks to Princess Diana. Fendi’s Baguette, meanwhile, outlived its early-aughts It-bag heyday and found a new generation of fans more than two decades later. Their enduring appeal speaks to the power of great design, which can transcend changing tastes, evolving trends, and creative director shake-ups.

Of course, a handbag doesn’t need decades of history behind it to become a wardrobe staple. Sometimes, an unexpected silhouette, celebrity endorsement, or clever design detail can turn a newcomer into a cult classic overnight. Identifying the forever pieces among today’s endless stream of new arrivals is then part of the fun.

Beyond the initial buzz, the most promising designs have some things in common: practical proportions, distinctive details, and versatility—all the more important when you’re considering a four-figure purchase. The best designer handbags should fit seamlessly into your wardrobe rather than demand an entirely new one. They should be flexible enough to carry everywhere from dinner to work and the grocery store, beautifully crafted to withstand years of wear, and stylish enough to elevate even the simplest of outfits.

Below, Vogue’s guide to the best designer handbags, from bona fide icons to established favorites and newer arrivals with the potential to become tomorrow’s most treasured pieces. Whether you're drawn to a heritage house signature or something less ubiquitous, these are the bags worth getting to know—and keeping close for years to come.

The Paddington was the bag of the mid-2000s, instantly recognizable for its slouchy shape and oversized padlock hardware. Worn by every It-girl from Kate Moss to Sienna Miller, it defined an era of bohemian glamour. In 2025, the cult bag returned under Chloé creative director Chemena Kamali, who has revived the padlock-topped icon in various sizes and colors.

Balenciaga’s Le City bag was a favorite of Noughties It-girls—think the Olsen twins, Nicole Richie, and Lindsay Lohan. It made a full-fledged comeback in 2024 with refreshed proportions and multiple colorways. Today, the archival icon endures as a house staple—equally tempting in its new iterations as vintage styles. While plenty of fashion lovers are reaching for the new model, which comes in a range of colorways, others, including British Vogue’s Naomi Smart, are securing their wishlist pieces second-hand on preloved sites such as eBay and Vinted.

Gucci’s Jackie is one of fashion’s true icons. Originally beloved by Jacqueline Kennedy Onassis, the hobo-shaped shoulder bag has been reissued countless times, each wave balancing retro charm with contemporary relevance. Modern versions—sleek, compact, and available in lush hues, as well as go-with-everything neutrals—make it just as covetable today as in the ’60s.

First introduced as Jonathan Anderson’s debut bag at Loewe, the Puzzle quickly became a fashion-insider favorite for its origami-like panels and clever, shape-shifting construction. Now, with Proenza Schouler founders Jack McCollough and Lazaro Hernandez as Loewe’s creative directors, the Puzzle remains a house cornerstone—offered in multiple sizes and colorways, with the classic full-size in black or beige still the chicest bet.

Miu Miu’s Aventure may feel in step with fashion’s current appetite for ladylike top handles, but the bag’s roots go back. Introduced for fall 2024, the softly structured style reimagines a doctor bag from the 2009 archives, complete with curved lines, a snap-hook closure, and vintage appeal. Since its debut, the Aventure has become one of Miu Miu’s most popular styles, offered in everything from nappa leather to suede and an ever-changing lineup of colors.

The Prada Passage bag may have only made its debut on the spring 2026 runway, but its architectural, slightly off-kilter silhouette already has the makings of a modern classic. The elongated style plays with contrasting textures and a clever bag-within-a-bag effect. With its folded sides, protruding flap, and slender handles, it’s practical, minimal, and guaranteed to become a must-have for collectors of the brand.

The Row has a knack for transforming familiar handbag silhouettes into instant must-haves, and the Agnes is no exception. Inspired by vintage bowling bags, the structured top handle is marked by its gently curved shape, tubular handles, flat base, and sweeping zip closure. Devoid of flashy logos or hardware, the Agnes features a quietly distinctive design that sets it apart—and feels destined to get even better with age.

Khaite is renowned for its arsenal of timeless, investment-worthy accessories. The brand's Blake bag reimagines the classic box silhouette with a softly structured, flap-front shape that combines clean lines with sculptural curves. The result is a contemporary crossbody that offers form and function. More recent Soft Blake styles loosen things up, translating the same understated elegance into a supple, slouchier shape designed for everyday wear.

Spotted on just about every cool girl, the Balenciaga Rodeo has quickly become one of fashion's defining It bags. Its slouchy silhouette draws inspiration from vintage briefcases, while a structured top handle and removable, adjustable leather strap allow it to be carried by hand, over the shoulder, or crossbody.

It was clear that the Empire bag was an instant hit upon walking into the Vogue offices—you can spot at least three perched on an editor’s desk at any given time. The appeal of this popular Coach style lies in its marriage of aesthetic and accessibility—its roomy design and mid-level price make it hard to ignore. Opt for the larger 40 model for daytime and the slightly more compact 35 for evenings.

First introduced in 2004 under then-creative director Tomas Maier, Bottega Veneta's Campana bag has been relaunched for fall 2025. The softly curved shoulder bag retains its signature Intrecciato weave and double handles, now with even sleeker lines. Its spacious silhouette and lack of hardware make it an effortless everyday option, while its two-decade history proves that some designs are timeless for a reason.

When Carrie Bradshaw slung a whipstitched Fendi baguette over her shoulder in Sex and The City, she helped turn the already-iconic bag into a worldwide sensation. And while the style has never really gone away, it has enjoyed a serious renaissance over the last decade, with a new generation discovering its Noughties charm. Recent re-editions, from tactile pony hair to richly embellished iterations, prove there’s still plenty of life left in the silhouette.

Originally introduced in the 1970s, Loewe's Amazona bag returned from the archives to mark the house's 180th anniversary. This medium-sized version is crafted in Spain from supple leather and finished with reinforced corners for added structure. True to its effortless appeal, it's designed to be carried slightly open—what Jonathan Anderson described as looking "like a chic mistake"—while a concealed closure keeps the contents secure. Removable shoulder and crossbody straps add to its versatility.

When Toteme introduced the T-Lock in 2022, the Swedish label proved its minimalist sensibility translated just as well to accessories as to ready-to-wear. Defined by a softly structured silhouette, curved flap, and instantly recognizable T-shaped clasp, the bag has since become a signature of the brand—and a favorite of celebrities like Katie Holmes. Available in everything from buttery leather to earthy suede, and in a range of sizes and colors, the T-Lock feels just as relevant today as it did four years ago—and promises to remain so for decades to come.

Saint Laurent’s Le 5 à 7 has become one of the house’s quintessential everyday bags, offered in both a sleek, subtly curved shoulder silhouette and a more spacious bucket shape. Its name nods to the Parisian “after-work to before-dinner” window, telegraphing day-to-night ease. Available in smooth or grained leather, suede, and seasonal finishes, both styles are discreet staples that read polished without trying.

Another iconic bag named after another iconic woman, Dior’s Lady Dior bag owes its fame to Princess Diana. Originally called the Chouchou, the boxy top-handle bag was gifted to Diana by then-First Lady of France, Bernadette Chirac, in September 1995. The princess quickly made it a signature, carrying it frequently to public engagements and requesting a version in blue to match her eyes. In 1996, Dior renamed the bag the Lady Dior in honor of its most famous fan. It remains one of the brand’s most popular bags.

Named for—and inspired by—the curved shape of its namesake French pastry, Lemaire’s Croissant has quickly become one of the house’s signatures. Curved panels give the crescent bag its memorable shape, allowing it to mold against the body when worn crossbody, while knotted strap ends and a looped zipper pull make for recognizable, playful finishes. Since launch, the line has expanded to include a variety of sizes and colorways.

Louis Vuitton’s Neverfull tote is often spotted on the arms of airport-bound celebrities, no doubt thanks to its practical, capacious interior (the clue is in the name) and timeless logo leather design. Introduced in 2007 as a beach bag, the style has experienced a revival in recent years.

Launched in the fall/winter 2022 collection, Miu Miu’s Wander bag has already secured its place in the designer bag hall of fame, thanks to its distinctive matelassé detailing and compact size. Beloved by the likes of Emma Corrin, Alexa Chung, Gigi Hadid, Hailey Bieber and Jaime Xie, to name but a few, its star shows no sign of fading.

Fashion-insider favorite accessories brand Savette built its name on retro-tinged ladylike handbags, but the Soft Symmetry takes the label’s codes in a more relaxed direction. Introduced in 2026, the roomy top handle trades the original Symmetry’s structure for a slouchier silhouette, generous interior, and dangling zipper tails that lend it an appealingly undone quality. Founder Amy Zurek designed it with longevity in mind: recognizable enough to feel distinctly Savette, but restrained enough to transcend a trend cycle.

Leave it to Prada to turn a humble, dust bag-like drawstring pouch into one of 2026’s most coveted accessories. Introduced on the spring 2026 runway, the Wish Pouch’s pared-back construction takes on a different look depending on the material: Silk duchesse versions come in jewel-box shades, while leather, nylon, and neutral iterations offer a more understated take on the whimsical silhouette.

Coach knows its way around a buzzy bag (see: the Bella Hadid-beloved Brooklyn), and Chelsea is already emerging as another hit. The roomy shoulder bag pairs a relaxed, soft shape with a flap closure and minimal hardware. Available in leather and suede, it has the easy, throw-it-over-your-shoulder appeal that makes a bag more likely to become a wardrobe mainstay than a one-season wonder.

Well, it shifts from season to season. For fall 2026, Prada is back on top: The Lyst Index crowned it the world’s hottest brand in Q3, with the house reclaiming the number one spot for the first time since 2023. Elsewhere, Gucci remained in the top five, Chloé climbed two places, and Bottega Veneta rose three spots following Louise Trotter’s much-anticipated debut for the house.

The season’s most-wanted bags offer an equally varied snapshot of what shoppers want right now. Prada’s silk duchesse Wish Pouch was Lyst’s hottest product of Q3, with searches surging 498 percent. Meanwhile, Balenciaga’s slouchy Rodeo landed at number eight, with the fashion platform calling out “a spectrum of slouchy top-handle bags” among the quarter’s strongest performers.

It bags like Toteme’s T-Lock Bag and Miu Miu’s Aventure have proved they have staying power beyond their initial buzz, while perennial signatures, including Saint Laurent’s Le 5 à 7 and Gucci’s Jackie, continue to make the case for investing in a silhouette with history behind it. At the same time, a new class of contenders is emerging: Savette has softened its signature polish with the relaxed Soft Symmetry, and The Row has put its typically minimalist spin on the vintage bowling bag with the Agnes.

The takeaway? There isn’t one handbag (or even one handbag aesthetic) dominating right now. The most compelling styles range from softly slouching carryalls to structured top handles and fanciful evening pouches. So ultimately, the smartest investment is the bag that works with your wardrobe and your life—and that you’ll still want to carry long after its moment on the Lyst Index has passed.

#6753. 13 Best Deodorant for Men 2026, According to Dermatologists

Frankly, the best deodorant for men sells itself. It stinks to stink: Body odor is right up there with bad breath as a totally avoidable misfortune. But while deodorant might seem like an odd category to get overly psyched about, as a longtime grooming editor, I can confidently say we're living in a golden age of the underarm essential.

Unlike the synthetic and chalky ghosts of deodorant sticks past, today’s best deodorants are a a sea of sophisticated formulas, improved textures, better scents, and naturally derived ingredients that, yes, actually work. The only hard part is honing in on the best one for you. Price, feel, skin sensitivity, and your sweat and odor levels matter. So I tested a whole lot of deodorants to narrow the field to seven standouts, some new, some tried-and-true, plus a few more deeper cuts I also loved.

I also tapped trusted dermatologists, for some expert insights further down. Just one last quick note: We’re not talking antiperspirants here, which primarily rely on aluminum compounds to reduce sweat. If that’s what you’re after, I’ve got recommendations for those, too.

Now, are there more targeted, more sophisticated, and, well, chicer deodorants on this list? Absolutely. But at the end of the day, you want your deo to do three things: keep the stink at bay, smell good, and be easy to repurchase. Dove Men+Care hits every mark, which is why it's in every drugstore.

The price, of course, is great, but then there's the scent: a surprisingly sophisticated blend of bright bergamot and warm white amber that's fresh, subtly citrusy, and softly warm. It smells so much better than your typical underarm fare and is actually a little mood-boosting, as the packaging suggests. The aluminum-free, baking-soda-free formula features moisture-attracting ingredients, giving it a little skincare credibility, too. It also feels super smooth going on, and kept its scent for most of the day. No notes!

Hip grooming brand Church California's deodorant only launched two years ago, but for me, it's everything a niche, forward-thinking deodorant should be: Effective, made with almost entirely naturally derived ingredients, and housed in compostable, plastic-free packaging. The formula uses magnesium and organic tapioca starch for odor and moisture control, with coconut oil and shea butter adding a little skin-conditioning goodness. And that scent? Wonderfully herbaceous, thanks to an essential oil blend that smells like the actual outdoors.

Admittedly, the sturdy cardboard tube takes a little getting used to—you push the stick up from the bottom instead of twisting a dial. And the glide is certainly a little less smooth. But oh, does the formula hold up. Even hours later, I'd catch little whiffs of those lovely botanicals, and when the scent eventually faded, there was still no detectable B.O. For the environmentally conscious guy, it's a no-brainer, and for the aesthete, it looks retro cool sitting on your medicine cabinet shelf.

Ursa Major’s Hoppin’ Fresh stick is a modern legend in the deo space. Among us grooming geeks, this au naturel-meets-elevated formula changed the underarm game when it launched in 2015. It was one of those early artisanal step-ups from drugstore fare, and it earned the hype with thoughtfully curated, foraged-sounding ingredients, a subtle, natural-smelling citrus scent, and a skincare-centric stick that glides on smoothly.

It still holds up today, fighting odor, soothing skin, and absorbing excess moisture to keep you smelling fresh. For an aluminum-free deo, it also keeps me pretty dry, too. And even the packaging—a sleek, solid-blue tube—feels like a style upgrade. Scent wise, in winter Forest Fix is the way to go. But the original Hoppin' Fresh is always waiting in the wings once the warmer months come around.

I'm well aware that Old Spice has plenty of newer, more fragrance-centric variations, many with names like Swagger. But I've always preferred the tried-and-true stuff, and that blue stick, here in High Endurance Refresh, is about as iconic as deodorant gets. It's my old reliable, and one I always keep as a backup, whether I'm visiting family, staying overnight somewhere, or just need something I can count on in a pinch. This classic has aged remarkably well, because it simply works.

Then there's the nostalgia, which hits me every time I catch a whiff of that distinctively fresh-meets-medicinal aroma I've loved unironically for years. The formula isn't particularly fancy: science-y ingredients give the aluminum-free stick its smooth glide, while glycerin adds a little skin-conditioning benefit. Would I wear this for an Ironman competition? Probably not. But for everyday errands, workdays, and just about everything in between? Absolutely. At under $15 for a three-pack, it's also easily one of the best value options on this list.

When you think gel deodorant, you probably picture those old-school perforated dispensers with tons of holes. But Baxter of California's is a smooth, transparent gel stick that's still, in my book, among the best. Part of the appeal is the formula, which packs some impressive botanicals: witch hazel and tea tree oil help tackle odor-causing bacteria, while chamomile helps soothe skin. Add tried-and-true glycerin to the mix, and you've got a gel deodorant with some serious skincare cred, too.

Then there's the application itself. The clear gel glides on effortlessly, with a cool, crisp, almost medicinal feel that's especially refreshing during the warmer months. Better still, it won't leave white marks on your shirts, something I always appreciate with my go-to black T-shirts. Is it the most heavy-duty odor fighter on this list? Not quite. But for everyday wear, it keeps the funk at bay without feeling like you've applied much of anything.

I test a lot of deodorants, but few become permanent fixtures in my bathroom. So it's worth telling you that Freaks of Nature's Everyday Endurance has become my primary deodorant lately. The brand may be known best for sunscreen, but it knows its way around our underarms too. And much like its sunscreens, part of the appeal is the application. The lotion-like formula emerges through a clever F-shaped grate, and there's something oddly satisfying about watching it dispense before smoothing it onto your underarms.

Better still, it absorbs well without any gunky, sticky residue. Cocoa butter and sunflower oil give it a skin-conditioning quality that makes this one of the most soothing deodorants I've ever worn. It's premium-priced, sure, but between the standout application, exemplary performance, and skin-conditioning feel, it's worth every penny.

Gone are the days when deodorant had to smell like “Sports Ice Rush.” Today's best odor fighters offer sophisticated, subtle scents (so they don't compete with your cologne), and Salt & Stone remains one of the top examples, with deodorants that have actual scent pyramids—Saffron & Cedar, Black Rose & Oud, Bergamot & Hinoki, for example. All are nuanced, refined, and never too loud.

But it's not just about the scent. The formula neutralizes odor and absorbs excess moisture very well, while skincare-centric additions like niacinamide and shea butter help keep underarms comfortable. More importantly, in my experience, the fragrance doesn't devolve into some funky olfactory murk by day's end. You still smell like the scent you applied that morning, or at the very least, fresh. Are these the heaviest-duty or most affordable deodorants out there? Nope. But they deliver on fragrance and function, and that's a combination worth investing in.

Caldera Lab just launched its first deodorant, and given the brand's skincare chops, it's no surprise the formula reads like a serum: niacinamide, aloe vera, and hyaluronic acid soothe and hydrate; postbiotics and magnesium tackle odor; and arrowroot absorbs moisture. Stacked, indeed.

Can Aesop do any wrong? Not really, and its deodorant spray is another example of the botanical-meets-aromatic goodness the amber-hued brand does so well. It's the only spray on this list, and while its odor protection holds up well, a midday refresh is sometimes warranted—and honestly, part of the pleasure.

If your skin is extra sensitive, Nécessaire's entire fragrance-free lineup is exemplary, and its deodorant stick is no exception. It keeps odor impressively in check, is easy on sensitive underarms, and won't compete with your favorite cologne. It's also aluminum- and baking soda-free, dermatologist-tested, hypoallergenic, and even carries the National Eczema Association's Seal of Acceptance.

Cremo may be kings of shave cream, but it knows a thing or two about deodorant, too. The formulas are affordable, the odor protection holds up, and the scents smell so damn good. Take Palo Santo, with its warm, woody, slightly smoky aroma that feels far more sophisticated than its price suggests. Coconut oil and shea butter add the skin-conditioning touch you'd expect from a pricier stick. rant quietly in the background, look elsewhere—but if you like a lot of fragrance with your funk-fighting, Cremo delivers serious bang for the buck.

The Grey's culty, rightfully hyped deodorant is the best old-school-style roll-on I've ever tried. The unscented formula is so lightweight you almost have to check you're applying anything, but oh, you are, and there's a cooling tingle as it goes on. It's the most expensive deodorant on this list, but with its premium slim aluminum casing and impressively lightweight formula, it's an investment in barely-there odor-fighting care.

Malin+Goetz's Eucalyptus Deodorant is a stone-cold classic that helped elevate gel sticks and make them feel refreshingly natural. The scent is practically a trademark at this point, equal parts medicinal, herbal, and oh-so-subtle. But there's substance behind it: eucalyptus extract helps refresh skin, while odor-neutralizing citronellyl methylcrotonate keeps the funk at bay.

As a grooming editor, I've tried more sticks, sprays, gels, and roll-ons than I can count, from drugstore staples to niche newcomers. And while plenty have impressed me on first swipe, the real test is whether I keep reaching for them weeks, months, or even years later.

Here, I drew on firsthand testing, focusing on odor protection, scent, texture, application, skin comfort, and, of course, how well they hold up. I've worn these deodorants through warm and cool weather, long days, and everything in between. Some are favorites I've relied on for years, while others are newer that are now part of my medicine cabinet rotation. As I've said, the best deodorant sometimes depends on the occasion or even the season, so it's a good idea to have a few on hand if possible. At the end of the day, a deodorant needs to keep B.O. at bay, ideally absorb excess moisture, and feel comfortable. Some excel in certain areas more than others, but each one above warrants its spot among the best deodorants.

Here is some dermatologist advice on deodorants—the best ingredients to look for, plus some controversial ones, too—with insights from board-certified dermatologists Kiran Mian, Ryan B. Turner, and Heather Rogers.

The primary cause of body odor is “bad” bacteria pairing up with sweat. There are two ways to prevent the stink: Reduce perspiration in the area, and/or create an inhospitable environment for the bacteria.

These are the most common ingredients to seek out if you want to temper the proliferation of bacteria in your pits (and anywhere you’re particularly pungent).

This antimicrobial and anti-inflammatory mineral safely and effectively kills bacteria without irritating skin, says Mian.

Dr. Mian also endorses the non-irritating magnesium hydroxide, a naturally occurring compound that neutralizes bacteria without absorbing into the skin.

“The terpenes in tea tree oil make this ingredient naturally antibacterial and antifungal, helping to reduce body odor,” Turner says. “In its pure, concentrated form, it can be very irritating. It’s best to use a product that’s formulated with tea tree oil at low percentages. It’s still effective when diluted, and a little bit goes a very long way.”

This one is controversial to some. Most skin types will tolerate baking soda (sodium bicarbonate) just fine, but only trust reputable, well-reviewed brands who use it. “Baking soda has a very alkaline pH level, while that of the skin is more acidic,” explains Turner. “This disrupts the skin’s natural barrier, harming the good bacteria in our microbiome, and leaving our skin more susceptible to irritation and inflammation.” (We’ve included a few deodorants with baking soda below, plus many natural picks that explicitly exclude it.)

It’s easy to get these two confused, but they share a principle. “Prebiotics feed the good bacteria on our skin (bacteria that does not break down sweat releasing a foils odor), which then overpopulates those odor-producing bacteria,” explains Mian. “Probiotics are the good bacteria that will ideally populate the skin and overtake odor causing bacteria.” The names of these might be strange to you, like lactobacillus acidophilus or saccharomyces ferment. Chances are, a brand will proudly tout their pre- and probiotics, so look for that indication instead.

“These chemical exfoliating ingredients help resurface the skin, which also strips away bacteria as well as removes the dead skin that bacteria break down, which causes body odor,” says Turner. And Dr. Rogers echoes the love: “Using acids to exfoliate the skin in our armpits helps rebuild the acidic mantle [which is compromised with age], leading to better control of bacterial growth and odor. Many acids work great; glycolic, lactic acid and mandelic acid are my favorites. Salicylic acid, a beta hydroxy acid, has a higher chance of irritation.”

“Activated charcoal can help to absorb sweat and help to neutralize odors,” says Turner.

Arrowroot powder, tapioca starch, and cornstarch are popular ingredients in aluminum-free deodorants, helping absorb excess moisture and keep underarms feeling dry without blocking sweat production. Of tapioca starch, Mian says, “This non-irritating starch won’t clog sweat ducts like aluminum, which can cause breakouts.” (It's also terrific in anti-chafe products for similar moisture-absorbing benefits.) “Like tapioca starch, corn starch pulls moisture from the skin to leave a powdery feeling behind. Unless you have an allergy to these plants, they are safer to use,” says Turner. Both doctors particularly favor arrowroot powder as a naturally derived, generally well-tolerated ingredient for absorbing moisture.

Both help soak up surface moisture without blocking sweat production. Freaks of Nature's formula includes bentonite clay.

A naturally occurring, porous mineral powder that absorbs excess moisture and helps keep underarms dry. You'll find it in Ursa Major's deodorant.

Approach your deodorant purchase with the following considerations:

While it’s easy to celebrate a fully natural formula—and for good reason—keep in mind that not all natural ingredients are inherently good for your skin. Ingredients like baking soda and certain essential oils can cause irritation, particularly if your underarms are sensitive. Conversely, synthetic ingredients aren't automatically bad for your skin, either. “What’s more important is to consider the manufacturer of the products—are they reputable? Do they perform extensive testing? What are the ingredients used and from where are they sourced?” says Turner. That's sound advice whether you're shopping natural or synthetic. There's a reason dermatologists frequently recommend established brands like Dove: They have the resources to develop, test, and manufacture formulas at scale, often at a fraction of the price of more niche alternatives. Of course, that doesn't mean smaller brands aren't doing their homework, either. Finding the right deodorant still takes some trial and error, gents, but you can always start with our list.

If your underarms are easily irritated, start with the ingredient list. Baking soda, strong fragrances, essential oils, and certain acids can trigger irritation, though everyone's skin reacts differently. Look for skin-conditioning ingredients like shea butter, glycerin, and aloe, several of which you'll find in the deodorants featured above. Fragrance-free formulas are a smart starting point for sensitive skin, while unscented are worth considering, too—just know that some contain masking fragrances.

Deodorants come in all sorts of formats these days, from classic solid sticks and clear gels to sprays, roll-ons, lotions, and pastes. How they feel when you apply them matters as much as how well they work. Some glide on more smoothly, while others feel chalkier, thicker, or more moisturizing. Gels and roll-ons tend to feel lightweight and refreshing (great for warmer weather), while richer lotions and pastes feel more nourishing and suit the cooler months. Ultimately, the best deodorant feels comfortable, doesn't leave residue on your clothes, and fits your lifestyle.

Dr. Kiran Mian is a board-certified dermatologist at Hudson Dermatology and Laser Surgery in NYC, and volunteer faculty at the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai University.

Dr. Ryan B. Turner is a board-certified dermatologist and founder of Turner Dermatology in NYC and the TRNR Skin skin care line.

Dr. Heather Rogers is a board-certified dermatologist and co-founder of Modern Dermatology in Seattle and the founder of the Doctor Rogers skin care line.

#6752. Everything We Know About ‘Black Doves’ Season 3

Black Doves, the sleek and sexy Netflix series about the complicated friendship between a spy played by Keira Knightley and an assassin played by Ben Whishaw, has returned for season 2. Already caught up? Not sure whether the long-term commitment is worth it? Here’s what we know about the odds that Black Doves will be renewed for season 3.

The first season brought Knightley’s character Helen, a spy married to a prominent conservative politician, back into action in the aftermath of her lover’s murder. The second season shoves her into the spotlight as her husband becomes prime minister. Meanwhile, in both seasons, Whishaw’s character Sam does his best to protect her while fighting his own demons, internally and externally. As various secret organizations and powers that be pull their strings to use them as pawns, the two of them can really only trust each other.

As of the season 2 release, Black Doves has not yet been renewed for season 3. The second season was announced before the first season dropped on Netflix. In theory, that’s concerning. But maybe the show was initially “ordered” for two seasons, and they announced it as an early renewal to create some well-deserved buzz before the premiere.

So far, season 2 reviews have been good. If the audiences follow, then we should (hopefully) get the good news soon.

No spoilers, but season 2 leaves a lot up in the air. Many of the characters are split up. Big secrets have been revealed. I wouldn’t be surprised if a third season went international again. Every story about a spy and/or assassin teaches us that you can’t escape your past.

However, since Black Doves is not based on a preexisting book series or film, it is difficult to decipher what happens next. That’s up to creator Joe Barton, who of course also created The Lazarus Project and recently adapted the play Amadeus to the small screen.

This is the thing. There were two years between Black Doves season 1 and season 2. That’s the problem with getting big movie stars to make television shows. Scheduling can be difficult.

But are we really going to have to wait until 2028 for Black Doves season 3? That would not be ideal. With all of the twists and turns of a show like this, you’ll need to do a total preseason series rewatch to remember what happened. If it is 2028, it’ll probably drop in November or December. That’s the one thing you can count on...this is a chilly series.

#6749. Ralph Lauren Pre-Fall 2027

Ralph Lauren picked up the Menswear Designer of the Year Award at the CFDAs earlier this week. He also took home the organization’s first men’s prize in 1981. That means—if I have my dates right—he’s been at the top of American fashion since before this year’s other winners were born. In an industry built on change, renewing and maintaining a legacy can be as difficult as building one, but even as he approaches the brand’s 60th anniversary, Lauren still has fashion’s attention. PoloFest, the vintage marketplace the company organized in Tokyo last month, with its 5,000 specially selected archival Polo pieces and 10,000 visitors, is bound to spawn imitators across the business.

This pre-fall collection wasn’t designed to make that kind of noise, but it’s as rooted in the brand’s iconography as anything else it does. Take the glen plaid pantsuit in look 3—it’s based on a suit that Lauren himself frequently wears and made by tailors in Italy with the specialized techniques that give men’s suiting its sharp lines and structure. The track pants in look 1 are another Ralph tic; he’s always liked mixing casual and formal, low and high. Purple is the accent color here this season, as it is across so much of fashion, alongside minty green, though we can’t blame the prevailing currents. Lauren pays no heed to trends. Case in point: The silvery plunge-front halter top is a lift from his own 1990s archives.

#6748. Bob Dylan Dressed Like Timothée Chalamet to Meet the Pope

Today, millions of Americans awoke to social media feeds awash with images of and commentary about a landmark event that seemed nigh-impossible a mere 24 hours earlier. I speak, of course, of this image:

As the nation began to digest the results of a historic election that seemed to herald the arrival of a new America, two of our very best Americans met for a private audience on the other side of the Atlantic: Bob Dylan, the Great American artist, and Pope Leo XIV, the first American Pope. Dylan is in the midst of yet another lengthy European tour—his strongest in some number of years, judging by recent bootleg tapes. On November 2, he played a show at Milan’s Unipol Dome, then jetted over to Rome ahead of a November 5 performance at the ​​Palazzo dello Sport. What better way to kill an off-day than a quick chat with the Vicar of Christ?

It wasn’t the first time Bob met a Pope, as some pointed out. In 1997, he performed for John Paul II at the World Eucharistic Congress in Bologna, donning a dapper Western suit and a fine Stetson for the occasion. He and JP2 made for a bit of an odd couple, the mysterious American gunslinger and the seemingly-nonplussed Polish holy man.

Dylan has somewhat more in common with Pope Leo, a.k.a Robert Francis Prevost, a fellow Midwesterner. But even if the two men hail from similar geography, the sight of them together under the bright fluorescent lights of an anonymous Vatican office looked like the product of a well-crafted AI prompt, if not an outright fever dream. The images were so unexpected, so uncanny, I would’ve been convinced they were fake had they not been published by an official press organ of the Vatican.

Much of the whiplash stemmed from the two men’s appearances. Angel and devil. Spy versus spy. The man in the long black coat and the man in the short white mozzetta. The one liners wrote themselves.

On Wednesday, the Pope wore a clean white cassock and a tidy little zucchetto, with an iron cross hanging down around his neck. In short, he looked like the Pope. I suppose I would say the same about Bob: that he looked like himself. As any good Dylan fan knows, however, the meaning of that phrase has changed radically over the years. Bob’s shifting appearance is almost as notorious as his shifting artistic sensibility. Dust bowl refugee, sharp-suited mod, bohemian poltergeist, whatever this is—the man has worn many hats.

A hoodied Timothée Chalamet, seen with Kylie Jenner, in New York City.

Sometime in the early 1990s, Dylan took a liking to the humble hoodie, a stylistic evolution that intersected neatly with his booze-fueled artistic nadir. The hoodie allowed him to hide in plain sight, even as he continued to take the stage around the world on his Never Ending Tour. It was practical, yes, but it was also a defense mechanism, a way to synthesize his compulsion to perform and his aversion to being seen. That it often looked hard as hell did not hurt. (It should come as little surprise that Timothée Chalamet, who may as well have been born wearing a hoodie, seemed to riff on this era when he was channeling Bob all those months ago.)

In the 21st century, Bob came unstuck from time. On landmark records like “Love And Theft” and Modern Times, Dylan burrowed into an imaginary musical past situated somewhere between the Civil War and the Great Depression. His style shifted to match. In the early aughts, he adopted a full country-western guise, complete with a Lee Van Cleef mustache. In the years that followed, his sartorial inspirations shifted east: a little less cowboy, a little more riverboat gambler, often performing in wide-brimmed hats, long frock coats, and string ties. “Rock and roll Mark Twain” wouldn’t have been an inaccurate descriptor.

Which brings us back to today’s meeting with Pope Leo. On first glance, Dylan’s ensemble is bonkers: western black blouson with contrast stitching along the chest and collar; beneath that, a heavyweight black hoodie zipped to the chest; beneath that, a white collared shirt with several buttons undone, collar loosely drawn together with a polka-dot cravat. The hood is decidedly up, stationed atop a black flat brim cap. In some shots, Bob can even be seen sporting leather gloves and an old-fashioned umbrella, which seems to double as a cane.

Part “Man in Black” sobriety, part rock star debauchery, with a dash of the hypebeast flavor from Timmy’s A Complete Unknown press tour—the man got a damn fit off in Vatican City. There’s no other way to describe it. (It’s a shame Pope Leo left his Rhude jacket back at the Papal Palace.)

Still, it’s a look with roots in Bob’s past, or pasts: the hoodies of the ’90s, the Westernwear of the 2000s, even the polka dots of 1965. No one but Bob would ever dare to pair all these disparate elements, particularly for a private audience with the Bishop of Rome. No one but Bob could.

Someone should come up with a word for that.

#6747. What Really Happened Between Sarah and John That Caused Their Divorce After ‘Love Is Blind’? A Much-Needed and Very Shocking Update

Love Is Blind Season 11 didn’t exactly go as planned for most of the engaged couples, with pretty much everyone breaking up before saying “I do.” But one pair managed to pull through! Sarah and John exchanged vows and got married (legally, I might add) during the Love Is Blind season finale.

“You are beautiful, you are brilliant, you are thoughtful, and I love you,” John said in his vows, while Sarah gushed “I love that you are sensitive and considerate and I find you funny.” Honestly, it was sweet!

The thing is...this finale was filmed over a year ago. Meaning, we’re in desperate need of an update on where Sarah and John stand today. Enter: the reunion! Netflix filmed the Love Is Blind reunion pretty recently, and there’s a shocking update on Sarah and John.

During an early reunion viewing on Tudum, John revealed he had an emotional affair about a year into the marriage, which led to their separation. "Unfortunately Sarah and I are no longer together, which is my fault,” John said. “We had a wonderful year of marriage, the two of us. Shared a lot of memories together. We had a wonderful year of marriage together, but unfortunately I made a mistake and there was a major breach of trust on my part. It's hard to talk about. There was a boys’ night I went on with a bunch of my friends and I just acted un-husbandly.”

He added that “nothing physical happened," and when pressed said “I texted one of the people we met out that night, and nothing happened, but she saw the texts and they were inappropriate for me to be sending as her husband. It was like three [texts], but they were bad.”

As for Sarah, she said the situation was “very sad,” that she'd struggled with “how John spoke to me” in the marriage, and that his behavior on the “boys’ night” was the "final thing that made me want to leave."

We don’t have information on where Sarah and John stand circa this moment, but it seems safe to assume they aren’t about to get back together given how the relationship ended.

#6744. Rag & Bone Pre-Fall 2027

The Rag & Bone team designs the label’s pre-fall collection in the peak of New York City’s summer. Observing the nuances of everyday dressing in the brand’s Meatpacking District neighborhood, Chief Merchandising & Design Officer, Jennie McCormick noted how the clothes blurred the distinction between day and night. In the showroom, she pointed to a dress with special detailing on the back and bias seams that flowed elegantly to the floor. “It could be worn around the city with a pair of sandals, but dressed up for an event at night,” she said. “One thing about the Rag & Bone woman is that she’s irreverent and she wears her dress because she just loves it.”

Matching sets have become a staple of the Rag & Bone wardrobe, and for pre-fall McCormick and co. offered some fun new takes. A mulberry silk utility tank and pants combo looked easy-wearing, while the printed organza set will give the R&B customer a dressed-up option without much effort.
