#6716. Your Horoscope for the New Moon in Scorpio

This lunation is bringing to the light everything that was done in the dark.

New Moons are a time for rejuvenation and manifestation. If you have a lack in your life, then this is the time the collective will work to fill it, whether through a new experience, person, or item. We must make space for beginnings and foolish behavior during new moons. Mind you, we’re all fools when beginning something new, so don’t be scared to get experimental.

For newbies, a New Moon is when the moon conjuncts the sun to the same degree. New moons are for setting intentions and goals to manifest. Take the theme of each new moon (manifestation period) as inspiration to bring forth the best version of yourself! If you find your horoscope helpful or have any questions, please share your horoscope and tag me on social media @monishaholmes.

The New Moon in Scorpio arrives Monday, November 9, 2026, at 2:02 a.m. ET, at 17 degrees Scorpio. I'm actually such a big fan of this new moon, because we're going to see a lot emerging from it—a lot more clarity. Things that were done in the dark are going to be exposed now. But don't expect everything to come out all at once, because new moons are dark for a reason. Look at the sky: it is not bright, it is a dark moon because the Moon sits between Earth and the Sun, meaning the side facing Earth receives no direct sunlight. In astrological terms, that means our emotions are too close to our sense of purpose, that we are not able to recognize how our feelings and ego are influencing life on Earth. We are going to see things unfolding over the next two weeks.This new moon is making a square to Mars, the planet of conflict and drive. A square is an astrological connection that represents friction—think about the phrase “squaring up.” You might be trying to get to the same goal as someone, but you can't exactly agree on how it's going to be done. We may be wanting something that is loud and bold and perhaps even radical. However, this new moon is testing our patience and basically saying “actually, wait.” We need to investigate. We need to understand what's going on before we can make big, dramatic, theatrical changes. We need to do the work of unearthing. Mars is also making a sextile with Venus retrograde in Libra, the last Venus retrograde that we're going to see like this in a while. When Mars sextiles Venus, what these two planets are doing is making a harmonious agreement: Mars is agreeing to expose if Venus is able to give justice, and Venus is willing to get harmony if Mars is willing to put things under a spotlight. This is going to be a very spicy new moon. If you expected boring, please know that boring is not going to be the theme of this week's moon.

Do not expect a downpour of information. We are not going to get a release of what is hidden immediately. Expect for things to take time to adjust, and then eventually information will start to unravel. If situations unfold fast then be careful, accelerated speed may indicate a potential crash out.

Retrogrades are about returns, reflections, re-evaluation. This isn't a time to make any huge, drastic changes or start something completely new. This is a time to look at what was done, how it is affecting us, so that we can begin to plan moving forward. And it's very important that we follow these steps.

Try to zoom out of yourself as the individual and think about what collective or communal justice would be. Perhaps you as an individual felt betrayed or overlooked or disappointed, but chances are, if it's happening in your neighborhood, then it's happening to somebody else on the block. So don't treat things as if they're occurring in isolation. In fact, wisdom comes from learning that very rarely are things happening to just one person.

Make sure that you are not acting out for the sake of acting out. This moon is calling for a sense of decorum, and considering that Pluto is the modern ruler of Scorpio this new moon’s theme is transformation. Currently, Pluto is direct in Aquarius, which means Pluto is governing change happening to the larger community. No change happens in isolation. We may not need huge masses of people to experience a breakthrough, but we do have to be strategic.

#6715. Why Are These Huge Arc’teryx Boots Suddenly Going Viral?

​Where were you during the Great Arc’teryx Jacket Phenomenon of 2022? If you’ve forgotten, the cult Canadian outdoors label went viral when young men on TikTok began filming themselves in the shower to demonstrate the hypnotic water-repelling ability of their Gore-Tex jackets. The attention only seemed to further cement Arc’teryx’s techy outerwear as an inescapable part of the menswear landscape. Now, the Vancouver brand appears to have another crossover hit on its hands: a hulking beast of a winter boot.

The Postour is a two-in-one design that combines a weatherproof outer boot with a removable insulated slipper tucked inside. In what the brand calls “full-boot mode,” the high collar cinches shut with a utility cord, sealing you off from the elements. The idea is that you can spend the day stomping through snow and slush, then shed the outer shell and lounge around in the slippers. Though it almost looks like a chalk bag sprouted a foot, the silhouette still carries the sleek, hyperfunctional minimalism the brand is known and loved for. The oddness of the design seems to be part of the appeal.

Naturally, it’s equipped with all the technical bells and whistles you’d expect from Arc’teryx: a gnarly Vibram Arctic Grip outsole, weatherproof Gore-Tex shell, and the label’s proprietary Coreloft insulation. Perhaps most covetably, there’s also a giant skeletal bird logo—known to diehards as the “deadbird”—on the side. The same logo has helped make the brand’s beanies a favorite of everyone from Timothée Chalamet to Frank Ocean.

Much like Arc’teryx’s Gore-Tex jackets before it, the Postour has become unmissable on the men’s side of the fashion algorithm. It’s a viral object of desire for a certain type of menswear guy fluent in microtrends. (This is hardly the first time we’ve seen a polarizing boot take over the algorithm, after all.) The is-this-ugly-or-cool discourse only adds fuel to the fire—and the fact that the boots resemble a sought-after design from Yeezy Season 8 certainly doesn’t hurt. TikTok and Instagram are chock full with videos of dudes excitedly unboxing their boots, blasting them with hoses, and customizing them with colored wax. As a result of all this digital buzz, the $300 boot has been drifting in and out of stock on the official Arc’teryx website. At one point last week, it was fully sold out; as of press time, only a couple of sizes remain in stock (though REI currently has a full size run).

Of course, winter footwear has its own pantheon of heavy hitters, from L.L.Bean’s iconic Bean Boot to Sorel’s felt-lined stompers and Timberland’s “40 Below” Super Boot. Whether the Postour will earn a place alongside those classics remains to be seen. For now, Arc’teryx has made the rare winter boot that’s as hyped up online as it is useful in a snowstorm. Good luck getting your hands on a pair.

#6714. Soho House’s New Tokyo Outpost Is a Maximalist, East-Meets-West Wonder

When the Soho House team first began considering their first-ever Japanese property in 2019, one challenge stood out above all—given their hybrid members’ club with rooms model, the hospitality brand’s Tokyo outpost would need to be all things to all people.

For long-time members touching down in the Japanese capital, it had to deliver a genuine sense of place, immersing them in the city’s creative scene and offering a taste of the local cuisine. For Tokyoites, meanwhile—especially those of an Anglophile persuasion, given Japan’s long-standing reverence for British tailoring, subcultures, and craft—the appeal lay in the opposite direction. With the wealth of exceptional Japanese restaurants and bars already on their doorstep, they’d be looking for a slice of that louche, convivial London clubbiness (and possibly a Sunday roast). On top of that, private members’ clubs are still a relatively foreign concept in Tokyo: the few equivalents that do exist tend to skew more corporate.

It was a tricky square to circle, but if Soho House Tokyo—which opened its doors this summer in the design-forward neighborhood of Aoyama, just a stone’s throw from the frenetic energy of Omotesando crossing—is anything to go by, they’ve pulled it off. Credit belongs in large part to Soho House design director Domhnall Nolan, a self-professed Japan obsessive whose six-year odyssey began before the pandemic hit and involved years of traveling back and forth to study the country’s vernacular architecture, interiors, and craft traditions. “One key thing we honed in on was Soho House being inherently maximalist and Japan having a reputation for minimalism—with Tokyo specifically having that contrast,” Nolan explains. “It’s a city of juxtaposition where you have beautiful moments of calm, and then it’s also extremely dense and chaotic. Everything we were doing was always thinking about that juxtaposition of a minimal detail, but a maximal execution.”

When I arrived a few months back straight off a long-haul morning flight, my brain was still sputtering through the fug of jetlag—though the friendly, laid-back welcome certainly took the edge off. Stepping through the discreet timber double doors off Minami-Aoyama, I discovered a moody, amber-lit reception space wrapped in gridded panels of handmade washi paper and a smart check-in desk swathed in glossy Kyoto lacquer. (Even the staff looked almost absurdly sharp, outfitted in custom Japanese denim uniforms created in collaboration with Onitsuka Tiger; at first glance, they may appear intimidatingly cool, but they’re universally lovely and excited to offer tips for what to check out in the surrounding neighborhood.) The mood, both in the design and the general philosophy, is delightfully irreverent: one corner houses a custom graphic-wrapped Japanese vending machine dispensing striped beach towels, while the walls feature tongue-in-cheek artworks painted to look like oversized Uniqlo and convenience-store receipts. If high design is treated as something of a religion in Tokyo, Nolan clearly wasn’t afraid to commit a little heresy.

From there, I headed up to my bedroom—an “Extra Large” that felt like stepping into the apartment of a well-traveled Tokyo art collector. Passing along corridors lined with further custom washi paper, this time in a shade of indigo inspired by Japanese denim, the doors opened onto a living and dining area bathed in a soothing matcha palette and framed by a wraparound balcony overlooking the Aoyama skyline. (Every single room has a balcony, it turns out—a real rarity here.) The devil is in the details: on a crimson-stained credenza sat a row of Japanese spirits, a cocktail shaker, a ceramic sake set—and, in a delightfully retro touch, a rotary phone. Moving through to the bedroom, a timber bed was dressed with a fringed throw woven from upcycled vintage kimono fabrics in the traditional sakiori style, while the sprawling bathroom featured slabs of striated green marble, speckled Nagoya floor tiles, and a freestanding tub stocked with Cowshed bath salts. Even more thoughtfully, a trio of herbal Ross J. Barr patches had been left out on the table, a lifesaver after my 14-hour flight—I reached for the Sleep variety, stuck them behind my ears, and collapsed onto the immaculate cotton sheets.

That attention to local design extends well beyond the headline suites, however; even the “Cosy” rooms are packed with craft details that are rich with backstory. Nolan tells me later that while putting together a mock-up bedroom back in 2023, he spotted a traditional Japanese jewelry box whose dappled lacquer finish caught his eye, which led him to Makino Urushi, a small family-run workshop in Kyoto. “We went to see their factory, which is a handful of people doing everything themselves,” Nolan recalls. “They have a base of three standard colors—black, gold, and red—and when they show you how they create the other shades, you see the incredible depths of color they get. At one point, someone suggested we could make it cheaper in China, and I said, ‘I’m not going to China to make a Japanese finish.’” That persistence paid off: those intricate dappled lacquer finishes now grace mirror frames and drawer fronts, alongside parquet flooring laid in an interlocking tatami-mat grid.

Anyway, despite slapping on those herbal Sleep Patches, my body clock remained wholly uncooperative. By around 9 a.m., I was still sitting in bed staring out at the foggy Tokyo skyline like Scarlett Johansson in Lost in Translation. Admitting defeat, I headed upstairs to explore the two club floors on the 13th and 14th levels, connected by a monumental timber spiral staircase. Here, Nolan’s East-meets-West tightrope walk is at its most nimble. The so-called Club Lounge is cocooned in glossy burgundy paneling inspired by traditional lacquerware, offset by vintage European and Japanese mid-century armchairs, shelves of vinyl records, and a ceiling paneled with woven sea-grass wallpaper and authentic tatami border trims. “I knew it wouldn’t be appropriate to put actual tatami flooring on the ceiling,” Nolan notes. “There’s a sensitivity to it that Japanese members appreciate.”

My favorite detail? Over at the bar, traditional ceramic roof tiles have been flipped vertically to clad the front counter in a ripple of glazed olive green—an especially wry, witty touch—while the 14th-floor bar pairs glowing Italian Murano chandeliers with handmade lanterns and a swirling ochre-and-green onyx bar top. It’s a lot, but it all comes together to form a pleasing, surprisingly serene whole.

Eventually settling into a low-slung velvet sofa, I ordered the traditional Japanese breakfast: a wooden tray bearing a flaky fillet of grilled salmon, sweet rolled tamagoyaki, sesame-dressed greens on chunky glazed earthenware, and miso soup in a turned wood cup. (It proved to be merely the opening salvo of an extraordinary culinary lineup across the house, but more on that shortly.)

Sufficiently fueled for the day, it was time to brave Aoyama, one of the most dangerous neighborhoods on earth for anyone with a weakness for archival fashion—a category into which, much to the disappointment of my accountant, I very much fall. The surrounding backstreets are a labyrinth of designer flagships and meticulously organized secondhand boutiques; I spent the afternoon darting between three different outposts of the designer resale shop Kindal before wandering through the nearby Issey Miyake mini-district, where the late designer’s sculptural fashion wonders occupy their own string of gallery-like storefronts. (Issey-san’s designs are also significantly cheaper here than in the West, though the stock available can be a little spotty depending on the time of the month.) Eventually, with my jet-lagged limbs about to give way, I walked into Kuu, a nearby Japanese head spa recommended to me by the front desk staff. There, a therapist subjected my scalp, neck, and shoulders to an hour of steam, warm water halos, and pressure-point massage so relaxing I practically sleepwalked back to my room, before collapsing for a catatonic afternoon nap feeling like a freshly steamed dumpling.

That evening, we reconvened for dinner in the private dining room tucked behind frosted glass pocket doors at the far end of the house brasserie. Interestingly, Nolan had originally envisioned an Asian-led concept for the restaurant before pivoting late in the process. “As we looked at everything we had in the house already, we thought, ‘We need something that’s very not Japanese to balance these things out,’” he says. The result is a menu that riffs on British comfort classics using hyper-seasonal Japanese produce: our table groaned under plates of crisp tempura courgette flowers and Yamayuri pork loin glazed in a sweet mead reduction, alongside silver cups of French fries and rounds of spicy Picantes. For pudding, slices of tart topped with jewel-like arrangements of green muscat grapes arrived, alongside coupes of soft-serve ice cream crowned with white miso-infused popcorn—an unpretentious and fabulously umami-rich triumph.

The following morning required an even more brutal wake-up call: a 4:20 a.m. departure for Toyosu Fish Market (an hour that Soho House regulars usually meet on the way to bed, not breakfast) accompanied by Soho House Tokyo’s tuna supplier for backstage access to the morning’s bluefin auction. Pulling up to the recently modernized market complex under a drizzly dawn, we were led through a series of Backrooms-esque corridors before finding ourselves right next to the auction floor, watching dozens of frosted bluefin carcasses lined up on wooden pallets under the fluorescent lights. Buyers in rubber boots moved briskly between the rows, using hooks and flashlights to inspect the fat marbling and ruby-red sheen of each tail cross-section before the rapid-fire hand-signal bidding began. Afterward, we ducked into the wholesale stalls to watch a crew wield sword-length knives to break down the colossal tuna loins with surgical precision—and this exact supply chain made its way onto Chef Shinohara’s sushi counter back at Aoyama hours later, where we enjoyed the tuna with freshly grated Shizuoka wasabi and several pitchers of chilled sake.

After lunch, I spent my final afternoon scoping out the wellness and rooftop spaces. Down on the 13th floor, the dual-zone wellness studio—a jewel box of copper-toned walls, carved timber, and a hand-painted gold ceiling—was in full swing; while the rest of my group admirably threw themselves into a dynamic Reformer Pilates session, after a 4 a.m. fish market excursion, I opted to admire the bespoke leather kettlebells strictly as decorative objects, matcha in hand. Instead, I headed out to the 4,000-square-foot rooftop terrace, where the real showstopper—an infinity-style pool tiled in a geometric grid of bespoke ceramic tiles—looked across the sprawling skyline toward Tokyo Tower. (On a clear day, you can even spot the snow-dusted silhouette of Mount Fuji.)

Sitting by that indigo-tiled rooftop pool as the late-afternoon sun dipped behind the high-rises, my Lost in Translation malaise had been entirely dispelled. In a city that can make even the most seasoned traveler feel like an outsider, Soho House has pulled off something pretty remarkable: a space that honors the rigor of Japanese craft while wrapping you in the heady and ever-so-slightly unruly embrace of a great London club. Another shiso Picante, please.

#6712. A Look Inside WELL/BEINGS’s ‘Bound by Nature’ Gala

On November 6, cultural leaders, philanthropists, and conservation advocates braved the rain in New York City for a worthy cause. That evening, WELL/BEINGS hosted its annual benefit dinner at Hearst Tower, bringing guests together to support conservation efforts in the most vital and vulnerable ecosystems across the Caribbean and the Bolivian Amazon.

The event, titled “Bound by Nature” this year, was hosted by actor, entrepreneur, and philanthropist Oliver Trevena, and presented by the nonprofit’s co-founders Amanda Hearst Rønning and Breanna Schultz. Throughout the night, attendees enjoyed live music, conservation storytelling, an exclusive auction of fine art, jewelry, and luxury experiences, as well as a specially curated culinary experience by celebrity chef Eduardo Garcia.

As nods to the marine and terrestrial environments, the sea of guests wore shades of blue and green, respectively.

The benefit sought to raise funds toward more than $800,000 in programmatic commitments WELL/BEINGS has made to 15 conservation partners for 2026 and 2027. The selected organizations, which include local and underserved groups, are working to protect wildlife, restore critical habitats, and strengthen communities in targeted areas.

During her opening remarks, Hearst Rønning underscored the importance of investing in the people closest to the ecosystems in need of protection: “That is why we support and amplify local leaders,” she said. “They know what needs to be done. Too often, what stands between them and doing it is support and funding.”

Schultz echoed that sentiment, reminding attendees of the lasting impact of their contributions: “Our partners fight every day to protect what we love. Tonight, we can give them the resources to keep going…what we save now is what the next generation will inherit.”

Since its founding, WELL/BEINGS has invested more than $3 million in conservation. The organization also operates under a 100 percent donation model, with its co-founders and Board of Directors separately covering core operating expenses so that public donations go directly toward the mission at hand.

The evening also marked the launch of the Caribbean Bioregional Hub, a new initiative connecting nine partner organizations across the region to strengthen collaboration and advance coordinated conservation efforts. The sky is the limit!

Ecleen Luzmila Caraballo is the weekend editor at ELLE who covers celebrity and culture news. She was previously a senior editor at Complex and has contributed to other publications including GQ and Nylon. Born and raised in New York City to Panamanian parents, she’ll take book recs in English, Spanish (and soon, German). Her interests include music, fashion, beauty, film, earth science, and the study of love. On her time off, you can find her with loved ones at an odd-hour movie showtime, baking, or sitting in silence near a high-fidelity sound system.

#6711. Breaking Down the ‘Black Doves’ Season 2 Ending

For all the international stakes of the Black Doves season 2 finale, the tensest moments really came down to family. Can any spy and/or assassin have a family, found or otherwise? Won’t they all have to kill or be killed in the end? Here’s where Helen (Kiera Knightley), Sam (Ben Whishaw), and Reed (Sarah Lancashire) stand at the end of Black Doves season 2.

This season, while Helen starts to wonder that she’s been sidelined as a “spy wife” and abandoned by Reed, Sam has been given a peculiar kill list by an organization called Kestrel. He has to check it off in order to avoid jail time, or worse, but the names all seem to be connected to the Black Doves of old. This leads Sam and Helen to learn more about Reed, their employer. Then, we learn in final episode that the last person on Sam’s list is Reed herself.

The finale drags out the penultimate episode’s cliffhanger at the beginning of the finale. As it turns out, even though Reed was the fourth and final person on Sam’s list, he did not kill her. He turned her in to Patrick (Sam Riley) alive. That was enough to satisfy his contract, pay his debt, keep him out of jail, and destroy the evidence that Patrick has against Helen. Allegedly, that is! I don’t trust him...

Sam then attends the funeral of Jerry (Samuel Barnett), the concierge he was sleeping with and had to murder because of this mess. There is truly no rest for the wicked.

The rival bird-themed agency that Patrick works for easily recruits the rogue Black Dove. She’s anxious to cause chaos again after getting sidelined to a desk gig.

Oh right... there is a political storyline on this show. It’s easy to forget that when most of the action revolves around spies and assassins who don’t necessarily color inside partisan lines. Ultimately, Helen’s husband’s summit didn’t even happen. Kestrel agents attacked the summit in order to kidnap the US Defense envoy Cecille (Neve Campbell), get Helen in a car alone with Wallace, and orchestrate a confrontation between Reed and Katia Chernov at the Black Doves headquarters.

Big twist alert! We learn in the finale that the Alexi Chernov’s wife is Reed’s long lost daughter “Vita” who she abandoned in the Soviet Union. She’s been secretly plotting this for a long time and aims to get back on her mother and expose the Black Doves. Unfortunately, she neither gets her revenge nor lives to try again. The trio of female assassins–Laila, Williams, and Eleanor–arrive to rescue Reed to get her out.

Katia gives Helen an ultimatum: kill the Prime Minister or their children’s nanny Marie, a Black Dove turncoat, will kill them. (We knew that Marie was associated with Reed at the end of season 1... but both I and Wikipedia thought she was her daughter. Egg on our face, eh?) That’s the only way, Katia says, to put an end to all of this. Seems unfair to Wallace, who as far as we know has done nothing wrong, but whatever. Jerry was also an innocent victim this season.

But Helen does not shoot her husband. Instead, she leaves him in a car park and drives away with Sam to rescue their twins while the other assassins are saving Reed. She does so with a decent amount of ease. Helen shoots Marie point-blank in the head, but then takes her children to safety.

The final episode certainly has its casualties. Katia kills Cecille, sure. I’ve already mentioned that Marie dies, and Katia as well. Dani also dies by grenade in an elevator. But more main characters survived than you may have expected.

At the end of the episode, Patrick stages a meet-cute with Helen and slips her his business card. It’s absolutely a threat. But Reed and Helen are reunited. She also sits down with Wallace and prepares to tell him some version of the truth.

How will he take it? Will Helen and Reed manage to use their skills for good? And will Sam manage to stay in Italy for good this time? Just about all of his friends have contracts to kill him... but what if they just ignore them for a while? Will Eleanor and Williams stay together? We’re going to need Black Doves season 3 to find out.

#6710. Is 'The Only Living Pickpocket in New York' Immediately the Best Watch Movie Ever?

There are plenty of great movie watches: James Bond’s OG Rolex Submariner, Hans Gruber’s Cartier Tank, or even Hamilton’s made-for-Interstellar Murph. But there are very few great watch movies that dig into the myriad layers of meaning that compel real-world collectors. In that way, The Only Living Pickpocket in New York, which rolled out to theaters nationwide on October 30, is a timepiece-lover’s dream movie.

In the film, John Turturro gives an Oscar-buzzy performance as Harry Lehman, an aging New York hustler who has scraped by for decades without evolving with the world around him. He doesn’t have a phone, dances to vinyl records, pays at diners with cash, and rents Barbara Stanwych movies (“tapes,” he calls them) from the public library for his wife.

Naturally, Harry is drawn toward watches, both for his personal use as items to steal. Along the way of The Only Living Pickpocket in New York, there’s a cornucopia of watches and Easter eggs for collectors to appreciate: Director Noah Segan meticulously selected a watch to fit every character’s personality. It matters deeply to Segan whether a character is wearing a vintage Rolex Explorer 1016 or a modern Hublot; and the movie even gets deep into the inner workings of timepieces. A pawn shop owner, played by Steve Buscemi, deems a Patek Philippe “fugazi” and shows Harry the lack of jewels in the movement. Watches, as totems of an analog world imbued with personal and cultural history, aren’t just a detail, but a vital motif.

It’s clear that The Only Living Pickpocket in New York could only come from a writer-director embedded in the hobby themselves. And, in the future, Segan, along with the dealer Adam Golden who sourced the pieces for the film, plans to bring these essential watches to auction for charity. GQ talked with Segan about how he chose the film’s array of timepieces, the state of his own collection, and why he would make a terrible watch salesman.

Noah Segan: That’s a great question. I wouldn’t presume to jump on anybody else’s intent in terms of watches. I think obviously there are a lot of watches in movies that have become iconic. The first kind-of-nice watch I ever got myself was a TAG Heuer Monaco because I was such a huge fan of Steve McQueen and Le Mans. There are obviously a lot of watches that are worn. I don’t know how often they get woven into a story, but in our case, our story is not just about time, but time changing, time running out, and that in combination with very physical things, tactile things. We’ve got a pickpocket, he’s tactile. He touches you. The idea of a totem and an object representing those things started feeling very important to me, and watches do that for me.

I would probably be a very bad watch salesman simply because I would want to keep all my favorites. So I think maybe collector is where I should stay, but I’ve always been a very, for lack of a better term, sort of analog guy. I still shoot film with a camera. I spin records. I live in an old house. The classic car in the movie is my old car.

I was lucky enough to grow up in an environment that appreciates the marriage of engineering and art and history. To me, that Venn diagram is a solid circle when it comes to wristwatches. These are objects that can be beautiful, they can be sophisticated, they can represent personal historic endeavors and also the macrocosm of historic feats.

The idea of what a watch means when you think of it in terms of The Dirty Dozen [a WWII-era field watch for soldiers commissioned by Britain from 12 iconic Swiss watchmakers] being there for the military or [Paul] Newman’s Rolex Daytona and its engraving on the back that says, “Drive Carefully Me.” All of a sudden you’re talking about something bigger than us, a celebrity, probably one of the biggest celebrities of all time who did something absolutely crazy, which was not being a movie star, but being a race car driver. And yet his wife still said, “Drive Carefully Me.” So there’s the personal, there’s the promotional, there’s the macro and the micro, and they all are fascinating to me.

Well, a close friend of mine is Adam Golden, who has a company called Menta, is actually a watch dealer who deals in very specific, unique vintage watches of great provenance.

In considering the watch for Harry, I really wanted something that could bridge the gap between a very useful tool and something of value. And that watch represents a lot for people in that respect. There was a time when Harry was a younger man, and that would have been a really good, valuable, useful tool for him to have. It’s an understated watch. It’s easy to read. It can last through whatever you throw at it on the streets in New York.

And yet today it’s something of incredible value financially and also incredible value to him because it is his watch. It has been a tool for him. And I couldn’t think of a better example than that Rolex 1016 to represent that combination of factors. And so Adam found us that watch and loaned it to us to wear.

We built the other watches in the movie around [the 1016]. Giancarlo Esposito plays Detective Warren, [Harry’s] foil and mirror image. He both helps Harry and is keeping an eye on him. He wears a Tudor Tuxedo, which shares a lot of, as we say in the watch game, DNA with something like a Rolex Explorer. In fact, it was made by the same company, and yet it’s just a little different.

Steve [Buscemi’s character] wears a thin, gold Rolex Cellini on a gold bracelet that, again, is something that would have been definitely a luxury item back in the day and is an even bigger luxury item today, but still represents something of an older time. Meanwhile, the watch Dylan [a young mobster played by Will Price] has, the Hublot, is considered today to be a very flashy, modern watch. It has a modern chronograph movement. It’s made with very present-day materials. And in fact, he’s not wearing it. It’s stuffed into his gym bag, and he says, “I only wear that when I go out to flex,” because it doesn’t represent a daily tool to him.

All of these things were designed and lent to us by Adam Golden to talk about who these characters were and to reflect something about the characters in a world where the physical items and the physical representation matter.

I can walk you through all of it! We also had some interesting newer watches. We worked with an incredible team at Oris, a brand that’s been around forever, but remains really relevant. Victoria Morolis, who plays Eve, wears Oris. She’s a sort of younger hero in the movie and a punk computer hacker. She’s wearing the Oris Roberto Clemente, which is a watch that is very old-school in a lot of ways, but made with very 2026 technology.

She was wearing her very own gold Cartier tank. She said, “I am going to do this.” And we all said, “Of course you are, because you are the boss.”

Well, I have a personal feeling about that because I have a lot of knowledge of this stuff. This is my hobby, right? So to me, when I look at a 1016, I see history, I see Tenzing Norgay summiting Everest, whether that’s the actual truth or not. I am applying that to my perspective. And I’m also thinking about elegance in terms of what I like to wear. I’m thinking about how it sits on my wrist. I’m thinking about the simplicity in the design. And I can also see how someone else would appreciate the exact same thing about the Hublot: the work that went into skeletonizing that dial, the complication of a chronograph movement, and the mixture of metals and materials to make it. So I see both sides of it. I think because it is something so personal, it goes on your body. I think what ends up mattering is how you interpret that and whether you believe that one is of more value to you than the other stylistically.

Well, I think it sort of speaks to Harry’s world quite a bit. Harry comes from a world where if someone looked like they had money, they probably had money, right? And if they had nice shoes, they probably had a nice watch. And if they had a nice watch, they probably had money in their pocket. And you could do that math, and maybe it wouldn’t always be right, but these were educated guesses. And now we live in a world where a gold watch is not necessarily a gold watch. A Patek Philippe, presumably one of the most recognizable objects of value, is not necessarily an object of value. And to put that on Harry, to put that on a guy whose job it is to steal watches is, among other things, really a statement about him. And I guess in a wider sense that the world is not always what we think it is.

I think for the businessman at the beginning, he obviously has lots of nice suits and lots of nice shoes and he lives in a tall building on the Upper East Side and he’s got a camel hair coat and works in a fancy office. There are all these reasons to think that this guy is fancy and makes money. He doesn’t carry cash. You know what I mean? He wears Aldens, as we know, a fancy shoe, but he wears a fake watch. I think it speaks to where the world is right now, which is that it isn’t about honesty or dishonesty. There are shades of gray, and we exist in a bit of a gray world.

Great question. I think he knows that it’s fake. I think there is a world now where people—and I don’t think it’s just for watches, I think it’s for a lot of things—where people believe that getting most of the way toward something is enough. So somebody says to this guy, “Hey, you made partner. Isn’t it time to buy a $20,000 watch?” And then the guy next to him goes, “You can buy a $400 watch that looks just as good as a $20,000 watch.” And this guy goes, “Great.” And that’s it—that’s as far as they go.

“Too many” is the answer to how many watches I have. But most of what is in my collection that’s important to me are watches that are not [necessarily] of significant financial value. I have a watch that belonged to each of my grandfathers that I had restored. And I did not have fancy grandfathers. These are watches that cost more to restore than they were worth, but are of incredible value to me. And a couple of my friends who I’ve worked with many, many times, my friends and mentors in movies have given me watches, and those are important to me because of that, because of where they came from and what they mean and the consideration that went into them.

Watches like Benrus, which is, again, not a Rolex-level name, but Benjamin Lazarus founded that company in New York, and that means something to me as a guy from New York. So there’s something significant there. There are a lot of newer watches that I’m fascinated with, whether it’s companies like Oris or smaller brands like Haven or Bernhardt, which I appreciate.

I mean, listen, I don’t own an Omega Speedmaster. I’d love to own a Speedmaster. I love what they’re doing with modern watches now, actually. I’d love to own a gold Rolex. I think there’s something really cool about a gold Rolex.

I don’t know what I would do if I had a Rolex 6542, a Bakelite Bezel GMT [from the ’50s], because those are the coolest-looking watches. But if you sneeze at it wrong, does the bezel crack? I can’t worry about that.

Yeah, and I don’t believe in that! I want to wear my watches.

#6709. The 9 Most-Wanted Accessories of Fall—and How to Style Them Now

Among all the standout pieces on our fall shopping lists, it was the accessories that emerged as the real heroes. Both the fall and spring collections placed a renewed emphasis on personal style, with accessories offering some of the most compelling ways to make a look your own.

A necklace becomes more personal with the addition of collected charms, while a blazer or knit takes on new character with a brooch pinned to its lapel. Just as important is how these accessories are worn. Consider the strand of pearls layered beneath a sheer knit at The Row, or the silk scarf fastened around the waist like a cummerbund, rather than tied around the neck, at Polo Ralph Lauren. Sometimes, the smallest styling decisions make the biggest impact.

What these accessories have in common, beyond their styling potential, is their desirability. Between the fashion month street style set, our editors' own wish lists and wardrobes, and the collections we've seen since the fall shows, a clear picture has emerged of the accessories everyone wants to wear. Below, we've rounded up the season's most coveted pieces, along with a styling formula for each. From tasseled loafers to sculptural earrings, consider this your guide to the finishing touches that make an outfit.

Never underestimate the styling power of a delicate white floral brooch. Chanel's iconic camellia appeared in both the fall and spring collections, inspiring showgoers throughout fashion month to pin their own floral flourishes onto jackets and coats. The accessory has also become a favorite among Vogue editors (myself included), thanks to its ability to transform even the simplest outerwear. To offset its inherent femininity, try pairing one with a graphic T-shirt and a tailored blazer.

If there was one shoe silhouette that dominated the season, it was the pump. Lace-up iterations from Marni and Prada were particularly covetable, bringing a tougher, more directional attitude to an otherwise ladylike classic. Their appeal extends well beyond the traditionally feminine dresser. Lean into their unconventional proportions with a pair of skirted trousers and a brightly colored knit.

This is one trend I've had particular fun experimenting with, not least because it can be achieved with a simple rectangular silk scarf. Fold it in half lengthwise, wrap it around your waist, and knot it at the back, keeping the front wide and flat. It's a small styling trick that has transformed my trousers and tailoring, lending even a plain white T-shirt a certain polish. For the full effect, take a cue from Polo Ralph Lauren and embrace tuxedo-inspired dressing, right down to the patent leather slip-ons.

Eclectic charm necklaces were everywhere on the fall runways, from Celine and Altuzarra to Dries Van Noten and Marni. But what makes this jewelry trend especially appealing is the opportunity to make it entirely your own. You could, of course, invest in a ready-made version from Celine, but there's something even more charming about collecting medallions, keepsakes, and pendants over time and stringing them together yourself. Let a classic khaki trench and a fluted skirt provide the perfect backdrop.

Of all the re-edition Fendi Baguettes that caught our attention this season, the tiger-print version stood out for its nostalgic appeal. After several seasons of leopard print—and a sprinkling of zebra in the resort collections—tiger stripes offer a fresh alternative within the animal-print family. The trick is to let the print do the talking. Pair a tiger-striped bag with sleek black separates, such as a leather trench, knit dress, and ballet flats.

Call it the Phoebe Philo effect: The oversized statement earring is back, this time in sculptural clusters and explosive, burst-like shapes. What makes these earrings particularly interesting isn't just their scale, but the nonchalance with which they're worn. Rather than saving them for special occasions, consider them a form of everyday extravagance. A pair can do wonders for an otherwise understated combination of white jeans, a leather jacket, and ankle boots.

One reliable measure of an accessory's desirability? How difficult it is to get your hands on one. The Row's Calden tassel loafers have proved particularly elusive, cementing the menswear-inspired silhouette as one of fall's most-wanted shoes. Their appeal lies in their versatility: polished enough for tailoring, yet relaxed enough for everyday wear. A lived-in denim-on-denim look is just one way to put them to work.

At The Row, a simple strand of pearls was worn beneath a sheer, long-sleeved turtleneck rather than over it. The effect was subtle, unexpected, and remarkably chic. It's precisely this kind of styling that has brought the classic pearl necklace back into focus, though there's still plenty to be said for the traditional double-wrapped strand. Look to jewelry favorites Chan Luu and Sophie Buhai, as well as Toteme, for modern interpretations of the heirloom staple. Pearls also played a key styling role in By Malene Birger's lookbooks and on Valentino's runway, further proving their renewed appeal.

Belts have long been an essential finishing touch, but this season, it's the details that deserve a closer look. At Tory Burch's fall show, woven leather belts replaced their smooth counterparts—a seemingly minor distinction that made all the difference. Removed from their usual coastal-prep context, braided belts take on a decidedly more downtown attitude. Try one threaded through a pair of relaxed corduroys, finished with a purple barn jacket for an unexpected pop of color.
